title: Book Ten (1812) — Chapter 22
paragraphs: Staggering amid the crush, Pierre looked around.
"Count Peter Kirilych! How did you get here?" said a voice.

Pierre looked round. Boris Drubetskoy, brushing his knees with his hand (he had probably dirtied them kneeling before the icon), came up to him smiling. Boris was elegantly dressed with a slightly military flair appropriate to a campaign. He wore a long coat and, like Kutuzov, had a whip slung across his shoulder.

Meanwhile Kutuzov had reached the village and seated himself in the shade of the nearest house, on a bench that one Cossack had run to fetch and another had hastily covered with a rug. An immense and brilliant suite surrounded him.
The icon was carried farther, accompanied by the crowd. Pierre stopped some thirty paces from Kutuzov, talking to Boris.
He explained his wish to be present at the battle and see the position.

"This is what you must do," said Boris. "I'll show you around the camp. You'll see everything best from where Count Bennigsen will be. I'm in attendance on him, you know; I'll mention it to him. But if you want to ride around the position, come with us. We're just going to the left flank. Then when we get back, please spend the night with me and we'll arrange a game of cards. Of course you know Dmitri Sergeevich? Those are his quarters," and he pointed to the third house in the village of Gorki.
"But I'd like to see the right flank. They say it's very strong," said Pierre. "I'd like to start from the Moskva River and ride around the whole position."
"Well, you can do that later, but the main thing is the left flank."
"Yes, yes. But where is Prince Bolkonsky's regiment? Can you show me?"
"Prince Andrew's? We'll pass it, and I'll take you to him."
"What about the left flank?" asked Pierre.

"To tell you the truth, between us, God only knows what shape our left flank is in," said Boris confidentially, lowering his voice. "It's not at all what Count Bennigsen intended. He meant to fortify that knoll quite differently, but..." Boris shrugged. "His Serene Highness wouldn't have it, or someone talked him out of it. You see..." But Boris didn't finish, because at that moment Kaisarov, Kutuzov's adjutant, came up to Pierre. "Ah, Kaisarov!" said Boris, addressing him with an easy smile. "I was just trying to explain our position to the count. It's amazing how his Serene Highness foresaw the French intentions!"
"You mean the left flank?" asked Kaisarov.
"Yes, exactly; the left flank is now extremely strong."

Though Kutuzov had dismissed all unnecessary people from the staff, Boris had managed to stay on at headquarters after the changes. He had attached himself to Count Bennigsen, who, like everyone Boris had ever attended, considered young Prince Drubetskoy an invaluable man.

In the higher command there were two sharply defined parties: Kutuzov's and Bennigsen's. Boris belonged to the latter, and while showing servile respect to Kutuzov, he skillfully created the impression that the old man wasn't up to much and that Bennigsen was running everything. Now the decisive moment of battle had come, when Kutuzov would either be discredited and power would pass to Bennigsen, or even if Kutuzov won, it would be felt that everything was Bennigsen's doing. In either case, many great rewards would be given for the next day's action, and new men would come to the fore. So Boris was full of nervous energy all day.

After Kaisarov, other people Pierre knew came up to him, and he hadn't time to answer all the questions about Moscow showered on him or to listen to everything they told him. All faces expressed excitement and apprehension, but it seemed to Pierre that the excitement in some of these faces was mainly about questions of personal advancement; his own mind, however, was occupied by the different expression he saw on other faces—an expression that spoke not of personal matters but of the universal questions of life and death. Kutuzov noticed Pierre's figure and the group gathered around him.
"Call him to me," said Kutuzov.
An aide told Pierre of his Serene Highness's wish, and Pierre went toward Kutuzov's bench. But a militiaman got there before him. It was Dolokhov.
"How did that fellow get here?" asked Pierre.

"He's a creature that worms his way in everywhere!" was the answer. "He was demoted, you know. Now he wants to claw his way back. He's been proposing some scheme or other and has crawled into the enemy's picket line at night... He's a brave fellow, though."
Pierre took off his hat and bowed respectfully to Kutuzov.
"I concluded that if I reported to your Serene Highness, you might send me away or say that you already knew what I was reporting, but then I wouldn't lose anything..." Dolokhov was saying.
"Yes, yes."
"But if I were right, I'd be rendering a service to my Fatherland, for which I'm ready to die."
"Yes, yes."
"And should your Serene Highness need a man who won't spare his skin, please think of me... Perhaps I may prove useful to your Serene Highness."
"Yes... yes..." Kutuzov repeated, his laughing eye narrowing more and more as he looked at Pierre.

Just then Boris, with his courtier's skill, stepped up to Pierre near Kutuzov and in the most natural manner, without raising his voice, said to Pierre as though continuing an interrupted conversation:
"The militia have put on clean white shirts to be ready to die. What heroism, Count!"
Boris clearly said this to Pierre intending to be overheard by his Serene Highness. He knew Kutuzov's attention would be caught by those words, and it was.
"What are you saying about the militia?" he asked Boris.
"Preparing for tomorrow, your Serene Highness—for death—they've put on clean shirts."
"Ah... a wonderful, a matchless people!" said Kutuzov; and he closed his eyes and swayed his head. "A matchless people!" he repeated with a sigh.
"So you want to smell gunpowder?" he said to Pierre. "Yes, it's a pleasant smell. I have the honor of being one of your wife's admirers. Is she well? My quarters are at your service."
And as often happens with old people, Kutuzov began looking around absent-mindedly, as if forgetting everything he wanted to say or do.
Then, evidently remembering what he wanted, he beckoned to Andrei Kaisarov, his adjutant's brother.
"Those verses... those verses of Marin's... how do they go? The ones he wrote about Gerakov: 'Lectures for the corps inditing'... Recite them!" said he, clearly preparing to laugh.
Kaisarov recited... Kutuzov nodded his head, smiling, to the rhythm of the verses.
When Pierre had left Kutuzov, Dolokhov came up to him and took his hand.

"I am very glad to meet you here, Count," he said aloud, regardless of strangers present, in a particularly resolute and solemn tone. "On the eve of a day when God alone knows who of us is destined to survive, I'm glad of this chance to tell you that I regret the misunderstandings between us and would wish you not to hold any ill feelings toward me. I beg you to forgive me."
Pierre looked at Dolokhov with a smile, not knowing what to say. With tears in his eyes, Dolokhov embraced Pierre and kissed him.
Boris said a few words to his general, and Count Bennigsen turned to Pierre and proposed that he ride with him along the line.
"It will interest you," he said.
"Yes, very much," replied Pierre.
Half an hour later Kutuzov left for Tatarinova, and Bennigsen and his suite, with Pierre among them, set out on their ride along the line.

title: Book Ten (1812) — Chapter 23
paragraphs: From Gorki, Bennigsen descended the highway to the bridge which, when they had looked at it from the hill, the officer had pointed out as the center of our position, and where rows of sweet-smelling new-mown hay lay by the riverside. They rode across that bridge into the village of Borodino and then turned to the left, passing a huge number of troops and guns, and came to a high knoll where militiamen were digging. This was the redoubt, as yet unnamed, which would later be known as the Raevsky Redoubt or the Knoll Battery, but Pierre paid no special attention to it. He didn't know it would become more memorable to him than any other spot on the plain of Borodino.

They then crossed the hollow to Semenovsk, where the soldiers were pulling the last logs from the huts and barns. Then they rode downhill and uphill, across a rye field trampled and beaten down as if by hail, following a track freshly made by the artillery over the furrows of plowed land, and reached some fleches that were still being dug.
* A type of entrenchment.

At the fleches, Bennigsen stopped and began studying the Shevardino Redoubt opposite, which had been ours the day before and where several horsemen could be seen. The officers said that either Napoleon or Murat was there, and they all gazed eagerly at this small group of riders. Pierre also looked at them, trying to guess which of the barely discernible figures was Napoleon. At last those mounted men rode away from the mound and disappeared.

Bennigsen spoke to a general who approached him and began explaining our entire troop positions. Pierre listened, straining every faculty to understand the essential points of the coming battle, but was dismayed to find that his mental capacity was inadequate for the task. He couldn't make sense of it. Bennigsen stopped speaking and, noticing that Pierre was listening, suddenly said to him:
"I don't think this interests you?"
"On the contrary, it's very interesting!" replied Pierre, not quite truthfully.

From the fleches they rode still further to the left, along a road winding through a thick, low-growing birch wood. In the middle of the wood, a brown hare with white feet sprang out and, frightened by the tramping of so many horses, grew so confused that it ran along the road in front of them for some time, attracting general attention and laughter. Only when several voices shouted at it did it dart to one side and disappear in the thicket. After going through the wood for about a mile and a half, they came out on a clearing where troops of Tuchkov's corps were stationed to defend the left flank.

Here, on the extreme left flank, Bennigsen talked at length and with great heat, and, as it seemed to Pierre, gave orders of great military importance. In front of Tuchkov's troops there was a high ground not occupied by troops. Bennigsen loudly criticized this mistake, saying it was madness to leave a height that commanded the surrounding country unoccupied, and to place troops below it. Some of the generals expressed the same opinion. One in particular declared with military passion that they had been placed there to be slaughtered. Bennigsen, on his own authority, ordered the troops to occupy the high ground. This decision on the left flank deepened Pierre's doubts about his own ability to understand military matters. Listening to Bennigsen and the generals criticize the position of the troops behind the hill, he fully understood them and shared their view—but for that very reason couldn't understand how the person who had placed them there behind the hill could have made so obvious a blunder.

Pierre didn't know that these troops were not, as Bennigsen supposed, placed there to defend the position, but were in concealment as an ambush—not meant to be seen—so they could strike an approaching enemy unexpectedly. Bennigsen didn't know this, and moved the troops forward according to his own ideas without consulting the commander in chief.

title: Book Ten (1812) — Chapter 24
paragraphs: On that bright evening of August 25, Prince Andrew lay propped on his elbow in a broken-down shed in the village of Knyazkovo at the far end of his regiment's camp. Through a gap in the broken wall he could see, beside the wooden fence, a row of thirty-year-old birches with their lower branches trimmed off, a field with sheaves of oats standing in it, and some bushes near which rose the smoke of campfires—the soldiers' kitchens.
Narrow and burdensome and useless to anyone as his life now seemed to him, Prince Andrew on the eve of battle felt as agitated and irritable as he had seven years before at Austerlitz.

He had received and given the orders for the next day's battle and had nothing more to do. But his thoughts—the simplest, clearest, and therefore most terrible thoughts—would give him no peace. He knew that tomorrow's battle would be the most terrible he had ever been in, and for the first time in his life, the possibility of death presented itself not in relation to any worldly matter or its effect on others, but simply in relation to himself, to his own soul—vividly, plainly, terribly, and almost as a certainty. And from the height of this awareness, all that had previously tormented and preoccupied him was suddenly illuminated by a cold white light without shadows, without perspective, without distinction. All of life appeared to him like magic-lantern pictures he had long been gazing at through a glass by artificial light. Now he suddenly saw those badly painted images in the clear daylight, without the glass. "Yes, yes! There they are, those false images that excited, enchanted, and tormented me," he said to himself, reviewing the principal pictures of the magic lantern of life and seeing them now in the cold white light of his clear perception of death. "There they are, those crudely painted figures that once seemed splendid and mysterious. Glory, the good of society, love of a woman, the Fatherland itself—how important these pictures seemed, with what profound meaning they appeared to be filled! And it is all so simple, pale, and crude in the cold white light of this morning I feel dawning for me." The three great sorrows of his life held his attention in particular: his love for a woman, his father's death, and the French invasion that had overrun half of Russia. "Love... that little girl who seemed to me overflowing with mysterious power! Yes, I loved her. I made romantic plans of love and happiness with her! Oh, what a fool I was!" he said aloud bitterly. "I believed in some ideal love that was to keep her faithful for the whole year of my absence! Like the gentle dove in the fable, she was to pine apart from me... But it was much simpler than that... It was all very simple and horrible."

"When my father built Bald Hills, he thought the place was his: his land, his air, his peasants. But Napoleon came and swept him aside, unconscious of his existence, as he might brush a chip from his path, and his Bald Hills and his whole life fell to pieces. Princess Mary says it is a trial sent from above. What is the trial for, when he is gone and will never return? He is gone! For whom then is the trial intended? The Fatherland, the destruction of Moscow! And tomorrow I shall be killed—perhaps not even by a Frenchman but by one of our own men, by a soldier firing a musket close to my ear, as one of them did yesterday—and the French will come and take me by the head and feet and fling me into a ditch so I won't stink under their noses, and new conditions of life will arise that will seem perfectly ordinary to others but about which I shall know nothing. I shall not exist..."

He looked at the row of birches shining in the sunshine, with their motionless green and yellow foliage and white bark. "To die... to be killed tomorrow... That I should not exist... That all this should still be, but not me..."

And the birches with their light and shade, the curly clouds, the smoke of the campfires, and everything around him changed and seemed terrible and menacing. A cold shiver ran down his spine. He rose quickly, went out of the shed, and began pacing.
When he returned, voices were heard outside the shed. "Who's that?" he called.

The red-nosed Captain Timokhin, formerly Dolokhov's company commander but now, due to the shortage of officers, a battalion commander, shyly entered the shed followed by an adjutant and the regimental paymaster.
Prince Andrew rose quickly, listened to the business they had come about, gave them additional instructions, and was about to dismiss them when he heard a familiar, lisping voice behind the shed.
"Devil take it!" said the voice of a man stumbling over something.

Prince Andrew looked out of the shed and saw Pierre, who had tripped over a pole on the ground and nearly fallen, coming his way. It was unpleasant to Prince Andrew to meet people from his own circle in general, and Pierre especially, for Pierre reminded him of all the painful moments of his last visit to Moscow.
"You? What a surprise!" he said. "What brings you here? This is unexpected!"

As he said this, his eyes and face expressed more than coldness—they expressed hostility, which Pierre noticed at once. He had approached the shed full of animation, but seeing Prince Andrew's face, he felt constrained and uncomfortable.
"I've come... simply... you know... come... it interests me," said Pierre, who had so often that day senselessly repeated the word "interesting." "I wanted to see the battle."

"Oh yes, and what do the Masonic brothers say about war? How would they stop it?" said Prince Andrew sarcastically. "Well, and how's Moscow? And my family? Have they reached Moscow at last?" he asked more seriously.
"Yes, they have. Julie Drubetskaya told me. I went to see them but missed them. They've gone to your estate near Moscow."

title: Book Ten (1812) — Chapter 25
paragraphs: The officers were about to leave, but Prince Andrew, apparently reluctant to be left alone with his friend, asked them to stay and have tea. Seats were brought and tea was served. The officers gazed with surprise at Pierre's huge, stout figure and listened to his talk about Moscow and the position of their army, around which he had ridden. Prince Andrew remained silent, and his expression was so forbidding that Pierre directed his remarks mainly to the good-natured battalion commander.
"So you understand the whole layout of our troops?" Prince Andrew interrupted him.
"Yes—that is, how do you mean?" said Pierre. "Not being a military man, I can't say I've fully understood it, but I get the general picture."
"Well then, you know more than anyone else, whoever that may be," said Prince Andrew.
"Oh!" said Pierre, looking over his spectacles in perplexity at Prince Andrew. "Well, and what do you think about Kutuzov's appointment?" he asked.
"I was very glad of his appointment, that's all I know," replied Prince Andrew.
"And tell me your opinion of Barclay de Tolly. In Moscow they're saying all sorts of things about him... What do you think of him?"
"Ask them," replied Prince Andrew, indicating the officers.
Pierre looked at Timokhin with the condescendingly inquiring smile that everyone involuntarily used when addressing that officer.
"We can see the light again since his Serenity's been appointed, your excellency," said Timokhin timidly, continually glancing at his colonel.
"Why so?" asked Pierre.

"Well, take just firewood and fodder, for example. Why, when we were retreating from Sventsyani, we didn't dare touch a stick or a wisp of hay or anything. You see, we were leaving, so he'd get it all; isn't that right, your excellency?" and Timokhin again looked at the prince. "But we didn't dare. In our regiment two officers were court-martialed for that kind of thing. But once his Serenity took command, everything became straightforward. Now we can see the light..."
"Then why was it forbidden?"
Timokhin looked about in confusion, not knowing how to answer. Pierre put the same question to Prince Andrew.

"So as not to lay waste the country we were leaving to the enemy," said Prince Andrew with bitter irony. "It's very sound: you can't allow the land to be pillaged or accustom the troops to looting. At Smolensk too he calculated correctly that the French might outflank us since they had larger forces. But he couldn't understand this," cried Prince Andrew in a shrill voice that seemed to escape him involuntarily: "he couldn't understand that there, for the first time, we were fighting for Russian soil, and that there was a spirit in the men such as I had never seen before, and that we had held the French for two days, and that that success had increased our strength tenfold. He ordered us to retreat, and all our efforts and losses went for nothing. He didn't intend to betray us; he tried to do his best; he thought out everything carefully—and that is exactly why he's unfit. He's unfit now precisely because he plans everything very thoroughly and precisely, as every German must. How can I explain it?... Well, say your father has a German valet, and the valet is excellent and satisfies your father's needs better than you could—then it's fine to let him serve. But if your father is mortally ill, you'll send the valet away and attend to your father with your own clumsy, unpracticed hands, and will comfort him better than a skilled stranger could. That's how it's been with Barclay. While Russia was healthy, a foreigner could serve her and be a splendid minister; but the moment she's in danger, she needs one of her own. But in your Club they've been calling him a traitor! They've slandered him as a traitor, and the only result will be that later, ashamed of their false accusations, they'll suddenly make him out to be a hero or genius instead—and that will be even more unjust. He is an honest and very meticulous German."
"And they say he's a skillful commander," Pierre remarked.
"I don't understand what 'a skillful commander' means," replied Prince Andrew ironically.
"A skillful commander?" said Pierre. "Well, one who foresees all possibilities... and anticipates the enemy's intentions."
"But that's impossible," said Prince Andrew, as if it were a long-settled matter.
Pierre looked at him in surprise.
"And yet they say war is like a game of chess?" he remarked.

"Yes," replied Prince Andrew, "but with this little difference: in chess you can think over each move as long as you like and aren't limited by time, and with this further difference, that a knight is always stronger than a pawn and two pawns are always stronger than one—while in war a battalion is sometimes stronger than a division and sometimes weaker than a company. The relative strength of bodies of troops can never be known to anyone. Believe me," he continued, "if things depended on plans made by the staff, I would be there making plans. But instead I have the honor of serving here in the regiment with these gentlemen, and I believe that on us—not on those others—tomorrow's battle will depend... Success never has depended, and never will depend, on position, equipment, or even numbers—and least of all on position."
"But on what then?"
"On the feeling that is in me and in him," he pointed to Timokhin, "and in every soldier."

Prince Andrew glanced at Timokhin, who looked at his commander in alarm and confusion. In contrast to his former reserved taciturnity, Prince Andrew now seemed stirred up. He apparently couldn't stop himself from expressing the thoughts that had suddenly taken hold of him.

"A battle is won by those who firmly resolve to win it! Why did we lose the battle of Austerlitz? Our losses were nearly equal to the French, but very early we told ourselves we were losing the battle—and we lost it. And we said so because we had nothing to fight for there, we wanted to get away from the battlefield as fast as possible. 'We've lost, so let's run,' and we ran. If we hadn't said that till evening, God knows what might have happened. But tomorrow we won't say it! You talk about our position—the left flank weak, the right flank overextended," he went on. "That's all nonsense, none of it matters. But what awaits us tomorrow? A hundred million totally unpredictable circumstances that will be decided in an instant by whether our men or theirs run or don't run, and whether this man or that man is killed. Everything being done now is just play. The fact is that those men you've been riding around with don't just fail to help—they actually hinder. They're only concerned with their own petty interests."
"At such a moment?" said Pierre reproachfully.

"At such a moment!" Prince Andrew repeated. "To them it's only an opportunity to undermine a rival and earn an extra medal or ribbon. For me, tomorrow means this: a Russian army of a hundred thousand and a French army of a hundred thousand have met to fight, and the point is that these two hundred thousand men will fight, and whichever side fights more fiercely and spares itself less will win. And if you want to know: whatever happens, whatever blunders those at the top may make, we will win tomorrow's battle. Tomorrow, happen what may, we will win!"

"That's right, your excellency! That's the truth, the real truth," said Timokhin. "Who would spare himself now? The soldiers in my battalion—believe me—won't touch their vodka! 'It's not the day for that!' they say."

Everyone fell silent. The officers rose. Prince Andrew went out of the shed with them, giving final orders to the adjutant. After they had gone, Pierre approached Prince Andrew and was about to start talking when they heard the clatter of three horses on the road nearby. Looking in that direction, Prince Andrew recognized Wolzogen and Clausewitz accompanied by a Cossack. They rode close by, still talking, and Prince Andrew involuntarily caught these words:
"The war must be extended across a wide area. I cannot praise that view highly enough," said one of them.
* "The war must be extended widely. I cannot sufficiently commend that view."
"Oh yes," said the other, "the only objective is to weaken the enemy, so of course one cannot take into account the loss of private individuals."
* "Oh yes, the only aim is to weaken the enemy, so of course one cannot consider the loss of private individuals."
"Oh, no," agreed the other.

"Extend widely!" said Prince Andrew with an angry snort when they had ridden past. "In that 'extend' were my father, son, and sister at Bald Hills. That's all the same to him! That's what I was telling you—those German gentlemen won't win the battle tomorrow, they'll only make as big a mess as they can, because they have nothing in their German heads but theories not worth an empty eggshell, and haven't in their hearts the one thing needed tomorrow—the thing Timokhin has. They've surrendered all of Europe to him, and now they've come to teach us. Fine teachers!" and again his voice went shrill.
"So you think we'll win tomorrow's battle?" asked Pierre.

"Yes, yes," answered Prince Andrew absently. "One thing I would do if I had the power," he began again, "I would not take prisoners. Why take prisoners? It's playing at chivalry! The French have destroyed my home and are on their way to destroy Moscow; they have outraged and continue to outrage me every moment. They are my enemies. In my view they are all criminals. And Timokhin thinks so too, and the whole army. They should be executed! Since they are my enemies, they cannot be my friends, whatever may have been said at Tilsit."
"Yes, yes," muttered Pierre, looking with shining eyes at Prince Andrew. "I completely agree with you!"

The question that had troubled Pierre on the Mozhaysk hill and throughout the day now seemed perfectly clear and fully resolved. He now understood the whole meaning and importance of this war and of the coming battle. Everything he had seen that day, all the significant and serious expressions on the faces he had passed, were illuminated for him by a new light. He understood that latent heat (as they say in physics) of patriotism which was present in all these men he had seen, and this explained why they all prepared for death calmly and almost lightheartedly.

"Not take prisoners," Prince Andrew continued. "That alone would completely change the whole war and make it less cruel. As it is, we've been playing at war—that's what's vile! We play at magnanimity and all that stuff. Such magnanimity and sensitivity are like a lady who faints at the sight of a calf being slaughtered: she is so tenderhearted she can't look at blood, but she enjoys eating the calf served up with sauce. They talk to us about the rules of war, about chivalry, about flags of truce, about mercy to the unfortunate, and so on. It's all rubbish! I saw chivalry and flags of truce in 1805; they deceived us and we deceived them. They plunder other people's homes, circulate counterfeit money, and worst of all they kill my children and my father—and then talk about rules of war and magnanimity to the enemy! Take no prisoners, kill and be killed! Whoever has come to this, as I have, through the same suffering..."

Prince Andrew, who had thought it made no difference to him whether Moscow was taken as Smolensk had been, was suddenly checked by an unexpected cramp in his throat. He paced back and forth a few times in silence, but his eyes glittered feverishly and his lips quivered as he began speaking.

"If there were none of this magnanimity in war, we would go to war only when it was worth going to certain death, as now. Then there would be no war because Paul Ivanovich had offended Michael Ivanovich. And when there was a war like this one, it would be real war! And then the determination of the troops would be completely different. Then all these Westphalians and Hessians whom Napoleon is dragging along would not follow him into Russia, and we would not go fight in Austria and Prussia without knowing why. War is not a polite game but the most horrible thing in life; and we ought to understand that and not play at it. We ought to accept this terrible necessity sternly and seriously. It all comes down to this: get rid of the falsehood and let war be war and not a game. As it is now, war is the favorite pastime of the idle and frivolous. The military profession is the most highly honored."

"But what is war? What is needed for success in warfare? What are the customs of the military? The aim of war is murder; the methods of war are spying, treachery, and their encouragement, the ruin of a country's inhabitants, robbing them or stealing to feed the army, and fraud and falsehood called military strategy. Military life means the absence of freedom—that is, discipline—plus idleness, ignorance, cruelty, debauchery, and drunkenness. And in spite of all this, it is the most esteemed class, respected by everyone. All the kings except the Chinese wear military uniforms, and the man who kills the most people gets the highest rewards."

"They gather, as we shall gather tomorrow, to murder one another; they kill and maim tens of thousands, and then hold thanksgiving services for having killed so many people (they even exaggerate the numbers), and announce a victory, supposing that the more people killed, the greater the achievement. How does God above look down at them and hear them?" exclaimed Prince Andrew in a shrill, piercing voice. "Ah, my friend, it has become hard for me to live of late. I see that I have begun to understand too much. And it isn't good for man to taste of the tree of knowledge of good and evil... Well, it won't be for much longer!" he added.
"However, you're sleepy, and it's time for me to sleep. Go back to Gorki!" said Prince Andrew suddenly.
"Oh no!" Pierre replied, looking at Prince Andrew with frightened, compassionate eyes.
"Go, go! Before a battle one needs a good night's sleep," repeated Prince Andrew.
He came quickly up to Pierre, embraced and kissed him. "Goodbye, be off!" he shouted. "Whether we meet again or not..." and turning away abruptly, he went into the shed.
It was already dark, and Pierre could not tell whether the expression on Prince Andrew's face was angry or tender.

For some time he stood in silence, wondering whether he should follow him or go away. "No, he doesn't want me to!" Pierre decided. "And I know that this is our last meeting!" He sighed deeply and rode back to Gorki.
Re-entering the shed, Prince Andrew lay down on a rug, but he could not sleep.

He closed his eyes. One image succeeded another in his imagination. On one of them he dwelt long and joyfully. He vividly recalled an evening in Petersburg. Natasha, with an animated, excited face, was telling him how she had gone looking for mushrooms the previous summer and had gotten lost in the big forest. She described the depths of the forest, her feelings, and a conversation with a beekeeper she met, incoherently and constantly interrupting her story to say: "No, I can't! I'm not telling it right; no, you don't understand," though he encouraged her by saying that he did understand, and he really had understood all she wanted to say. But Natasha was not satisfied with her own words: she felt they didn't convey the passionately poetic feeling she had experienced that day and wished to share. "He was such a delightful old man, and it was so dark in the forest... and he had such kind... No, I can't describe it," she had said, flushed and excited. Prince Andrew smiled now the same happy smile as he had then when he looked into her eyes. "I understood her," he thought. "I not only understood her, but it was that inner, spiritual force—that sincerity, that openness of soul—that very soul of hers, which seemed bound by her body—it was that soul I loved in her... loved so deeply and happily..." and suddenly he remembered how his love had ended. "He didn't need anything like that. He neither saw nor understood anything of the kind. He only saw in her a pretty, fresh young girl with whom he didn't bother to join his fate. And I?... and he is still alive and happy!"
Prince Andrew jumped up as if someone had burned him, and again began pacing back and forth in front of the shed.

title: Book Ten (1812) — Chapter 26
paragraphs: On August 25, the eve of the battle of Borodino, Monsieur de Beausset, prefect of the French Emperor's palace, arrived at Napoleon's quarters at Valuevo with Colonel Fabvier—the former from Paris, the latter from Madrid.

Putting on his court uniform, Monsieur de Beausset ordered a box he had brought for the Emperor to be carried before him and entered the first compartment of Napoleon's tent, where he began opening the box while chatting with Napoleon's aides-de-camp.
Fabvier did not enter the tent but stayed at the entrance talking to some generals he knew.

Emperor Napoleon had not yet left his bedroom and was finishing his morning grooming. Snorting and grunting slightly, he presented now his back and now his plump, hairy chest to the brush with which his valet was rubbing him down. Another valet, with his finger over the mouth of a bottle, was sprinkling Eau de Cologne on the Emperor's pampered body with an expression that seemed to say he alone knew where and how much cologne should be applied. Napoleon's short hair was wet and matted on his forehead, but his face, though puffy and yellow, expressed physical satisfaction. "Go on, harder, go on!" he muttered to the valet rubbing him, slightly twitching and grunting. An aide-de-camp, who had come to report the number of prisoners taken in yesterday's action, was standing by the door after delivering his message, awaiting permission to withdraw. Napoleon, frowning, looked at him from under his brows.

"No prisoners!" he said, repeating the aide's words. "They are forcing us to exterminate them. So much the worse for the Russian army... Go on... harder, harder!" he muttered, hunching his back and presenting his fat shoulders.
"All right. Send in Monsieur de Beausset, and Fabvier too," he said, nodding to the aide-de-camp.
"Yes, sire," and the aide vanished through the tent door.
Two valets quickly dressed His Majesty, and wearing the blue uniform of the Guards, he walked with firm, rapid steps to the reception area.

De Beausset's hands meanwhile were busy arranging the present he had brought from the Empress on two chairs directly facing the entrance. But Napoleon had dressed and come out so unexpectedly fast that de Beausset hadn't had time to finish preparing the surprise.

Napoleon noticed at once what they were up to and guessed they weren't ready. Not wanting to deprive them of the pleasure of surprising him, he pretended not to see de Beausset and called Fabvier over, listening silently and with a stern frown to Fabvier's account of the heroism and devotion of the troops fighting at Salamanca, at the other end of Europe, with but one thought—to be worthy of their Emperor—and but one fear—to displease him. The result of that battle had been disastrous. Napoleon made ironic remarks during Fabvier's report, as if he had never expected matters to go otherwise in his absence.
"I must make up for that in Moscow," said Napoleon. "I'll see you later," he added, and summoned de Beausset, who by then had prepared the surprise, covering something on the chairs with a cloth.
De Beausset made a deep bow—that courtly French bow which only the old servants of the Bourbons knew how to make—and approached, presenting an envelope.
Napoleon turned to him cheerfully and pulled his ear.
"You've hurried here. I'm very glad. Well, what is Paris saying?" he asked, suddenly changing his former stern expression to one of great cordiality.
"Sire, all Paris regrets your absence," replied de Beausset, as was expected.
But though Napoleon knew de Beausset had to say something like this, and though in his lucid moments he knew it was untrue, he was pleased to hear it. Again he honored him by touching his ear.
"I'm very sorry to have made you travel so far," he said.
"Sire, I expected nothing less than to find you at the gates of Moscow," replied de Beausset.
Napoleon smiled and, raising his head absent-mindedly, glanced to the right. An aide approached with gliding steps and offered him a gold snuffbox, which he took.

"Yes, it has worked out well for you," he said, raising the open snuffbox to his nose. "You love to travel, and in three days you will see Moscow. You surely didn't expect to see that Asiatic capital. You will have a pleasant trip."
De Beausset bowed gratefully at this acknowledgment of his taste for travel (of which he had not till then been aware).
"Ha, what's this?" asked Napoleon, noticing that all the courtiers were looking at something hidden under a cloth.
With courtly skill, de Beausset half-turned and, without showing his back to the Emperor, stepped back two paces, whisked off the cloth, and said:
"A present to Your Majesty from the Empress."
It was a portrait, painted in bright colors by Gerard, of the son born to Napoleon by the daughter of the Emperor of Austria—the boy whom everyone for some reason called "the King of Rome."

A very pretty curly-haired boy with a look of the Christ child in the Sistine Madonna was depicted playing with a stick and ball. The ball represented the globe and the stick in his other hand a scepter.

Though it was not entirely clear what the artist meant by showing the so-called King of Rome stabbing the earth with a stick, the allegory apparently seemed to Napoleon—as it had to everyone who had seen it in Paris—perfectly clear and very pleasing.
"The King of Rome!" he said, pointing to the portrait with a graceful gesture. "Admirable!"

With the natural ability of an Italian to change his facial expression at will, he stepped closer to the portrait and assumed a look of pensive tenderness. He felt that what he now said and did would be historic, and it seemed best for him—whose greatness enabled his son to play ball with the globe—to display, in contrast to that grandeur, the simplest paternal tenderness. His eyes grew misty, he stepped forward, glanced around for a chair (which seemed to place itself beneath him), and sat down before the portrait. At a single gesture, everyone tiptoed out, leaving the great man alone with his emotion.

After sitting still for a while, he touched—himself not knowing why—the thick spot of paint representing the highest highlight in the portrait, rose, and sent for de Beausset and the officer on duty. He ordered the portrait to be carried outside his tent so that the Old Guard stationed around it might have the pleasure of seeing the King of Rome, the son and heir of their adored monarch.

And while he was doing Monsieur de Beausset the honor of breakfasting with him, they heard—as Napoleon had anticipated—the rapturous cries of the officers and men of the Old Guard who had rushed to see the portrait.
"Long live the Emperor! Long live the King of Rome! Long live the Emperor!" came the ecstatic cries.
After breakfast, Napoleon dictated his order of the day to the army in de Beausset's presence.
"Short and energetic!" he remarked when he had read over the proclamation he had dictated straight off without corrections. It ran:

Soldiers! This is the battle you have so longed for. Victory depends on you. It is essential for us; it will give us all we need: comfortable quarters and a speedy return to our country. Behave as you did at Austerlitz, Friedland, Vitebsk, and Smolensk. Let our remotest posterity recall your achievements this day with pride. Let it be said of each of you: "He was in the great battle before Moscow!"
"Before Moscow!" repeated Napoleon, and inviting Monsieur de Beausset, who was so fond of travel, to accompany him on his ride, he went out to where the horses stood saddled.
"Your Majesty is too kind!" replied de Beausset to the invitation; he wanted to sleep, couldn't ride, and was afraid of trying.
But Napoleon nodded to the traveler, and de Beausset had to mount. When Napoleon came out of the tent, the cheering of the Guards before his son's portrait grew still louder. Napoleon frowned.
"Take him away!" he said, pointing with a gracefully majestic gesture to the portrait. "It is too soon for him to see a battlefield."
De Beausset closed his eyes, bowed his head, and sighed deeply, to show how profoundly he appreciated the Emperor's words.

title: Book Ten (1812) — Chapter 27
paragraphs: On the twenty-fifth of August, so his historians tell us, Napoleon spent the entire day on horseback, inspecting the terrain, considering plans submitted by his marshals, and personally giving orders to his generals.

The original Russian line along the river Kolocha had been disrupted by the capture of the Shevardino Redoubt on the twenty-fourth, and part of the line—the left flank—had been pulled back. That part was not entrenched, and in front of it the ground was more open and level than elsewhere. It was obvious to anyone, military or civilian, that this was where the French should attack. It would seem that no great deliberation was needed to reach this conclusion, nor any special effort on the part of the Emperor and his marshals, nor any need for that supreme quality called genius which people are so ready to attribute to Napoleon; yet the historians who described the event later, and the men who surrounded Napoleon at the time, and Napoleon himself, all thought otherwise.

Napoleon rode across the plain, surveyed the terrain with a profound air and in silence, nodded approvingly or shook his head dubiously, and without explaining to the generals around him the deep course of reasoning behind his decisions, merely gave them his final conclusions as commands. Having heard a suggestion from Davout (now called the Prince of Eckmuhl) to turn the Russian left wing, Napoleon said it should not be done, without explaining why. To a proposal by General Campan (who was to attack the fleches) to lead his division through the woods, Napoleon agreed, though the so-called Duke of Elchingen (Ney) ventured to remark that a move through the woods was dangerous and might throw the division into disorder.

After inspecting the terrain opposite the Shevardino Redoubt, Napoleon pondered briefly in silence and then indicated where two batteries should be placed by the next morning to act against the Russian entrenchments, and where the field artillery should be positioned in line with them.
After giving these and other orders, he returned to his tent, and the battle plan was written down from his dictation.
These dispositions, which French historians write about with enthusiasm and other historians with deep respect, were as follows:
At dawn the two new batteries established during the night on the plain occupied by the Prince of Eckmuhl will open fire on the opposing batteries of the enemy.

At the same time the commander of the artillery of the 1st Corps, General Pernetti, with thirty cannon of Campan's division and all the howitzers of Dessaix's and Friant's divisions, will move forward, open fire, and bombard the enemy's battery, against which will operate:
24 guns of the Guard artillery, 30 guns of Campan's division,
and 8 guns of Friant's and Dessaix's divisions—
in all 62 guns.

The commander of the artillery of the 3rd Corps, General Fouche, will place the howitzers of the 3rd and 8th Corps, sixteen in all, on the flanks of the battery that is to bombard the entrenchment on the left, which will have forty guns in all directed against it.
General Sorbier must be ready at the first order to advance with all the howitzers of the Guard artillery against either entrenchment.
During the cannonade, Prince Poniatowski is to advance through the wood on the village and turn the enemy's position.
General Campan will move through the wood to seize the first fortification.
After the advance has begun in this manner, orders will be given in accordance with the enemy's movements.

The cannonade on the left flank will begin as soon as the guns on the right wing are heard. The sharpshooters of Morand's division and of the Viceroy's division will open heavy fire when they see the attack begin on the right wing.

The Viceroy will occupy the village and cross by its three bridges, advancing to the same heights as Morand's and Gerard's divisions, which under his command will be directed against the redoubt and fall into line with the rest of the forces.
All this must be done in good order, retaining troops in reserve as far as possible.
The Imperial Camp near Mozhaysk,
September 6, 1812.

These dispositions, which are very vague and confused if one allows oneself to regard the arrangements without religious awe of Napoleon's genius, consisted of four directives—four different orders. Not one of them was, or could be, carried out.

The dispositions say first that the batteries placed at the spot Napoleon chose, together with Pernetti's and Fouche's guns (102 in all), were to open fire and bombard the Russian fleches and redoubts. This could not be done, because from the spots Napoleon selected, the shells could not reach the Russian works, and those 102 guns fired into the air until the nearest commander, contrary to Napoleon's instructions, moved them forward.

The second order was that Poniatowski, advancing on the village through the wood, should turn the Russian left flank. This could not be done and was not done, because Poniatowski, advancing through the wood, met Tuchkov there blocking his way, and could not and did not turn the Russian position.

The third order was: General Campan will move through the wood to seize the first fortification. Campan's division did not seize the first fortification but was driven back, because on emerging from the wood it had to re-form under grapeshot—something Napoleon hadn't foreseen.

The fourth order was: The Viceroy will occupy the village (Borodino) and cross by its three bridges, advancing to the same heights as Morand's and Gerard's divisions (for whose movements no directions are given), which under his command will be directed against the redoubt and fall into line with the rest of the forces.

As far as one can make out—not so much from this unintelligible sentence as from the Viceroy's attempts to execute it—he was to advance from the left through Borodino to the redoubt while Morand's and Gerard's divisions advanced simultaneously from the front.

All of this, like the rest of the plan, was not and could not be executed. After passing through Borodino, the Viceroy was driven back to the Kolocha and could get no farther; while Morand's and Gerard's divisions did not take the redoubt but were beaten back, and the redoubt was only captured at the end of the battle by cavalry (something probably unforeseen and unheard of by Napoleon). So not a single order in the plan was, or could be, carried out. But the dispositions state that after the fight begins in this manner, orders will be given according to the enemy's movements—and so it might be supposed that Napoleon would make all necessary adjustments during the battle. But this was not and could not be done, because throughout the entire battle Napoleon was so far away that (as later became clear) he could not follow the battle's progress, and not one of his orders during the fight could be carried out.

title: Book Ten (1812) — Chapter 28
paragraphs: Many historians say that the French did not win the battle of Borodino because Napoleon had a cold, and that if he hadn't had a cold, the orders he gave before and during the battle would have been even more brilliant, and Russia would have been lost and the face of the world changed. To historians who believe that Russia was shaped by the will of one man—Peter the Great—and that France became an empire and French armies marched into Russia by the will of one man—Napoleon—saying that Russia was saved because Napoleon had a bad cold on the twenty-fourth of August may seem logical and convincing.

If it had depended on Napoleon's will whether to fight or not fight the battle of Borodino, and if this or that arrangement had depended on his will, then obviously a cold affecting the exercise of his will might have saved Russia—and consequently, the valet who forgot to bring Napoleon his waterproof boots on the twenty-fourth would have been the savior of Russia. Along that line of reasoning, such a conclusion is indisputable, as indisputable as the conclusion Voltaire jokingly drew (not knowing what he was joking about) when he said that the Massacre of Saint Bartholomew was caused by Charles IX's upset stomach. But to people who do not accept that Russia was formed by the will of one man, Peter I, or that the French Empire was created and the war with Russia begun by the will of one man, Napoleon, that argument seems not merely untrue and irrational but contrary to all human reality. To the question of what causes historic events, a different answer presents itself: the course of human events is predetermined from above—it depends on the combined wills of all who take part in those events, and a Napoleon's influence on their course is purely superficial and illusory.

Strange as it may seem at first glance to suppose that the Massacre of Saint Bartholomew was not caused by Charles IX's will, though he gave the order and thought it was done because of his order; and strange as it may seem to suppose that the slaughter of eighty thousand men at Borodino was not due to Napoleon's will, though he commanded the battle's commencement and conduct and thought it happened because he ordered it; strange as these assumptions appear, human dignity—which tells me that each of us is, if not more, at least not less of a man than the great Napoleon—demands that we accept this answer, and historical investigation abundantly confirms it.
At the battle of Borodino, Napoleon shot at no one and killed no one. That was all done by the soldiers. Therefore it was not he who killed people.

The French soldiers went to kill and be killed at Borodino not because of Napoleon's orders but by their own volition. The whole army—French, Italian, German, Polish, and Dutch—hungry, ragged, and weary of the campaign, felt at the sight of an army blocking their road to Moscow that the wine was drawn and must be drunk. Had Napoleon then forbidden them to fight the Russians, they would have killed him and gone on to fight the Russians, because it was inevitable.

When they heard Napoleon's proclamation offering them, as compensation for mutilation and death, the words of posterity about their having been in the battle before Moscow, they cried "Long live the Emperor!"—just as they had cried "Long live the Emperor!" at the sight of the portrait of the boy poking the globe with a toy stick, and just as they would have cried "Long live the Emperor!" at any nonsense that might be told them. There was nothing left for them to do but cry "Long live the Emperor!" and go fight, in order to win food and rest as conquerors in Moscow. So it was not because of Napoleon's orders that they killed their fellow men.

And it was not Napoleon who directed the course of the battle, for none of his orders were carried out and during the battle he did not know what was happening in front of him. So the way these people slaughtered one another was not decided by Napoleon's will but happened independently of him, according to the combined will of the hundreds of thousands of people who took part in the common action. It only seemed to Napoleon that it all occurred by his will. And so the question whether he had or hadn't a cold has no more historical importance than the cold of the lowliest transport soldier.

Moreover, the claim by various writers that his cold was the reason his battle plans were not as skillful as on previous occasions and his orders during the battle were not as good as before is quite groundless—which again shows that Napoleon's cold on the twenty-sixth of August was insignificant.

The battle plans cited above are not at all worse but are actually better than previous plans by which he had won victories. His orders during the battle were also no worse than before—they were much the same as always. These plans and orders only seem inferior because the battle of Borodino was the first Napoleon did not win. The most profound and excellent plans and orders seem very bad, and every armchair strategist criticizes them with an air of importance, when they relate to a battle that was lost; and the very worst plans and orders seem brilliant, and serious people fill entire volumes proving their merits, when they relate to a battle that was won.
The battle plan drawn up by Weyrother for the battle of Austerlitz was a model of perfection—yet it too was criticized, precisely for its perfection, for its excessive detail.

Napoleon at the battle of Borodino fulfilled his role as the figurehead of authority as well as—and even better than—at other battles. He did nothing harmful to the battle's progress; he deferred to the most reasonable opinions; he caused no confusion, did not contradict himself, did not panic or run from the battlefield, but with his great tact and military experience calmly and with dignity played his part of appearing to command.

title: Book Ten (1812) — Chapter 29
paragraphs: Returning from a second inspection of the lines, Napoleon remarked:
"The chess pieces are set up — the game begins tomorrow!"

He ordered punch and summoned de Beausset, then began talking to him about Paris and about changes he planned to make in the Empress's household, surprising the prefect with his memory for the most minute details of court life.

He showed interest in trivial matters, joked about de Beausset's love of travel, and chatted carelessly — the way a famous, supremely confident surgeon does while rolling up his sleeves and putting on his apron as a patient is being strapped to the operating table. "The matter is in my hands and perfectly clear in my mind. When the time comes to act, I shall do it as no one else could, but for now I can joke, and the more I joke and the calmer I appear, the more reassured and confident you should feel, and the more you should marvel at my genius."

After finishing his second glass of punch, Napoleon went to rest before the serious business he believed awaited him the next day. He was so preoccupied with the task that he couldn't sleep, and despite his cold — which had worsened from the evening dampness — he went into the main section of the tent at three in the morning, blowing his nose loudly. He asked whether the Russians had withdrawn, and was told that the enemy's fires were still in the same places. He nodded in approval.
The adjutant on duty came into the tent.
"Well, Rapp, do you think we'll do good business today?" Napoleon asked him.
"Without doubt, sire," replied Rapp.
Napoleon looked at him.
"Do you remember, sire, what you did me the honor of saying at Smolensk?" Rapp continued. "The wine is poured and must be drunk."
Napoleon frowned and sat silent for a long time, leaning his head on his hand.

"This poor army!" he suddenly remarked. "It has shrunk so much since Smolensk. Fortune is frankly a courtesan, Rapp. I have always said so and I'm beginning to experience it. But the Guards, Rapp — the Guards are intact?" he asked questioningly.
"Yes, sire," replied Rapp.

Napoleon took a lozenge, put it in his mouth, and glanced at his watch. He wasn't sleepy and it was still nowhere near morning. It was impossible to give further orders just to kill time — they had all already been given and were now being carried out.
"Have the biscuits and rice been distributed to the Guard regiments?" Napoleon asked sternly.
"Yes, sire."
"The rice too?"

Rapp replied that he had passed along the Emperor's order about the rice, but Napoleon shook his head in dissatisfaction, as if not believing the order had been carried out. An attendant came in with punch. Napoleon ordered another glass brought for Rapp and silently sipped his own.

"I have neither taste nor smell," he remarked, sniffing at his glass. "This cold is unbearable. They talk about medicine — what good is medicine when it can't cure a cold! Corvisart gave me these lozenges but they don't help at all. What can doctors cure? Nothing. Our body is a machine for living. It's designed for that — it's its nature. Let life proceed in it without interference and let it defend itself; it will do more than if you cripple it by loading it with remedies. Our body is like a perfect watch that should run for a set time; the watchmaker can't open it — he can only adjust it by fumbling, and that blindfolded. Yes, our body is simply a machine for living — that's all."
And having started down the path of definition — which he enjoyed — Napoleon suddenly and unexpectedly offered a new one.
"Do you know, Rapp, what military art is?" he asked. "It is the art of being stronger than the enemy at a given moment. That's all."
Rapp made no reply.

"Tomorrow we'll have to deal with Kutuzov!" said Napoleon. "We shall see! Do you remember at Braunau he commanded an army for three weeks and never once mounted a horse to inspect his trenches? We shall see!"

He looked at his watch. It was still only four o'clock. He didn't feel sleepy. The punch was finished and there was still nothing to do. He got up, paced back and forth, put on a warm overcoat and a hat, and went out of the tent. The night was dark and damp, with a barely perceptible moisture falling from above. Nearby, the campfires of the French Guards burned dimly, and in the distance the Russian campfires glowed through the smoke. The weather was calm, and the rustle and tramp of French troops already beginning to move into position could be clearly heard.

Napoleon walked in front of his tent, looking at the fires and listening to the sounds. As he passed a tall guardsman in a shaggy cap standing sentinel before his tent — a man who had drawn himself up like a black pillar at the sight of the Emperor — Napoleon stopped in front of him.
"What year did you enter the service?" he asked, with the affected military bluntness and friendliness he always used when addressing soldiers.
The man answered the question.
"Ah! One of the old ones! Has your regiment had its rice?"
"It has, Your Majesty."
Napoleon nodded and walked away.
At half past five Napoleon rode to the village of Shevardino.
It was growing light, the sky was clearing, and only a single cloud lay in the east. The abandoned campfires were burning themselves out in the faint morning light.

On the right, a single deep cannon blast rang out and died away in the prevailing silence. Some minutes passed. A second and a third report shook the air, then a fourth and a fifth boomed solemnly nearby on the right.
The first shots had not yet finished reverberating before others rang out, more and more of them mingling with and overtaking one another.
Napoleon and his retinue rode up to the Shevardino Redoubt, where he dismounted. The game had begun.

title: Book Ten (1812) — Chapter 30
paragraphs: Returning to Gorki after seeing Prince Andrew, Pierre ordered his groom to have the horses ready and to wake him early in the morning, then immediately fell asleep behind a partition in a corner Boris had given up to him.
Before he was fully awake the next morning, everyone had already left the hut. The windowpanes were rattling and his groom was shaking him.
"Your excellency! Your excellency! Your excellency!" he kept repeating insistently while shaking Pierre by the shoulder without looking at him, apparently having lost all hope of waking him up.
"What? Has it begun? Is it time?" Pierre asked, waking up.
"Listen to the firing," said the groom, a discharged soldier. "All the gentlemen have gone out, and his Serene Highness himself rode past long ago."

Pierre dressed hastily and ran out to the porch. Outside everything was bright, fresh, dewy, and cheerful. The sun, just breaking through a cloud that had hidden it, shone with rays still half-blocked by clouds — over the roofs of the street opposite, the dew-spattered dust of the road, the walls of the houses, the windows, the fence, and Pierre's horses standing before the hut. The roar of guns sounded more clearly outside. An adjutant accompanied by a Cossack passed by at a brisk trot.
"It's time, Count; it's time!" cried the adjutant.

Telling the groom to follow him with the horses, Pierre walked down the street to the knoll from which he had surveyed the battlefield the day before. A crowd of military men had gathered there; staff members could be heard speaking in French, and Kutuzov's gray head in a white cap with a red band was visible, his gray neck sunk between his shoulders. He was looking through a field glass down the road ahead.

Climbing the steps to the knoll, Pierre looked at the scene before him, spellbound by its beauty. It was the same panorama he had admired from that spot the day before, but now the whole area was full of troops and covered by clouds of gun smoke, and the slanting rays of the bright sun, rising slightly to the left behind Pierre, cast penetrating streaks of rosy, golden-tinted light and long dark shadows across it all. The distant forest seemed carved from some precious yellowish-green stone; its undulating outline stood silhouetted against the horizon, pierced beyond Valuevo by the Smolensk road packed with troops. Closer by, golden cornfields glittered, interspersed with clusters of trees. Troops were visible everywhere — in front, to the right, and to the left. It was all vivid, majestic, and unexpected; but what struck Pierre most was the view of the battlefield itself — Borodino and the hollows on both sides of the Kolocha.

Above the Kolocha, at Borodino and on both sides of it — especially to the left where the Voyna River flows between its marshy banks into the Kolocha — a mist had spread that seemed to melt, dissolve, and become translucent as the brilliant sun appeared, magically coloring and defining everything. The gun smoke mingled with this mist, and across the whole expanse, through the haze, the morning sun's rays were reflected — flashing like lightning off the water, the dew, and the bayonets of troops massed along the riverbanks and in Borodino. A white church was visible through the mist, along with rooftops in Borodino, and dense masses of soldiers, green ammunition chests, and artillery pieces. And all of this moved — or seemed to move — as the smoke and mist spread over the entire space. Just as in the fog-filled hollow near Borodino, so along the entire line beyond it — and especially in the woods and fields to the left, in the valleys and on the hilltops — puffs of powder smoke kept springing up seemingly from nowhere, now individually, now in clusters, some translucent, others dense, swelling, growing, rolling, and merging, until they covered the whole panorama.
These puffs of smoke and — strange to say — the sound of the firing created the chief beauty of the scene.
"Puff!" — suddenly a round compact cloud of smoke appeared, shifting from violet to gray to milky white, and "boom!" came the report a second later.
"Puff! Puff!" — two clouds rose, pushing into each other and blending together; and "boom, boom!" came the sounds confirming what the eye had seen.

Pierre glanced back at the first cloud, which he'd seen as a round compact ball, and in its place floated balloons of smoke drifting to one side, and — "puff" (with a pause) — "puff, puff!" three and then four more appeared, and from each, at the same interval — "boom — boom, boom!" came fine, firm, precise sounds in reply. It seemed as though those smoke clouds sometimes raced and sometimes stood still while woods, fields, and glinting bayonets flew past them. From the left, across fields and bushes, large balls of smoke kept appearing followed by their solemn reports, while closer still, in the hollows and woods, small cloudlets burst from muskets — too quick to form full balls, but each with its own little echo. "Trakh-ta-ta-takh!" came the rapid crackle of musket fire, irregular and feeble compared to the cannon reports.

Pierre wanted to be there — amid that smoke, those gleaming bayonets, that movement and those sounds. He turned to look at Kutuzov and his staff, to compare his own impressions with theirs. They were all watching the battlefield as he was, and it seemed to him, with the same feelings. All their faces now shone with the latent warmth Pierre had noticed the day before and had fully understood after his conversation with Prince Andrew.
"Go, my dear fellow, go — and Christ be with you!" Kutuzov was saying to a general beside him, without taking his eye from the battlefield.
Having received this order, the general passed by Pierre on his way down the knoll.
"To the crossing!" the general said coldly and sternly in reply to a staff officer who asked where he was going.
"I'll go there too! I'm going too!" thought Pierre, and he followed the general.

The general mounted a horse a Cossack had brought him. Pierre went to his groom who was holding his horses and, asking which was the calmest, clambered onto it, grabbed it by the mane, and turning out his toes pressed his heels against its sides. Feeling his spectacles slipping off but unable to let go of the mane and reins, he galloped after the general — making the staff officers on the knoll smile as they watched him.

title: Book Ten (1812) — Chapter 31
paragraphs: Having descended the hill, the general Pierre was chasing turned sharply to the left, and Pierre, losing sight of him, galloped into ranks of infantry marching ahead. He tried to pass them on the right or the left, but soldiers were everywhere, all with the same preoccupied expressions, busy with some unseen but clearly important task. They all stared with dissatisfied, questioning looks at this heavyset man in a white hat who, for some unknown reason, threatened to trample them under his horse's hooves.
"Why are you riding into the middle of the battalion?" one of them shouted at him.
Another poked his horse with the butt of a musket, and Pierre, leaning over his saddlebow and barely able to control his shying horse, galloped ahead of the soldiers to an open space.

There was a bridge ahead, where other soldiers stood firing. Pierre rode up to them. Without realizing it, he had reached the bridge across the Kolocha between Gorki and Borodino, which the French — having occupied Borodino — were attacking in the first phase of the battle. Pierre saw that there was a bridge in front of him and that soldiers were doing something on both sides of it and in the meadow, among the rows of freshly mown hay he hadn't noticed through the campfire smoke the day before; but despite the incessant firing, he had no idea this was the actual battlefield. He didn't notice the bullets whistling from every side or the projectiles flying over him, didn't see the enemy on the other side of the river, and for a long time didn't notice the killed and wounded, though many fell near him. He looked about him with a smile that never left his face.
"Why is that fellow in front of the line?" somebody shouted at him again.
"To the left! Keep to the right!" men shouted at him.
Pierre went to the right and unexpectedly ran into one of Raevsky's adjutants, whom he knew. The adjutant looked angrily at him, clearly about to shout, but recognizing Pierre he simply nodded.
"How did you get here?" he said, and galloped on.
Pierre, feeling out of place, with nothing to do, and afraid of getting in someone's way again, galloped after the adjutant.
"What's happening here? May I come with you?" he asked.
"One moment, one moment!" the adjutant replied, and riding up to a stout colonel standing in the meadow, delivered some message, then turned to Pierre.
"Why have you come here, Count?" he asked with a smile. "Still curious?"
"Yes, yes," Pierre agreed.
But the adjutant turned his horse and rode on.
"It's tolerable here," he said, "but on the left flank with Bagration, they're taking a frightful pounding."
"Really?" said Pierre. "Where is that?"
"Come along with me to our knoll. We can get a view from there, and at our battery it's still bearable," said the adjutant. "Will you come?"
"Yes, I'll come with you," Pierre replied, looking around for his groom.

It was only now that he noticed wounded men staggering along or being carried on stretchers. In the very meadow he had ridden across the day before, a soldier lay sprawled across the rows of sweet-smelling hay, his head thrown awkwardly back, his cap fallen off.
"Why haven't they carried him away?" Pierre was about to ask, but seeing the grim expression on the adjutant's face as he too looked that way, Pierre held his tongue.
Pierre couldn't find his groom and rode along the hollow with the adjutant toward Raevsky's Redoubt. His horse lagged behind the adjutant's and jolted him at every step.
"You don't seem very used to riding, Count," the adjutant remarked.
"No, it's not that — her gait just seems so jerky," Pierre said in a puzzled tone.
"She's been wounded!" said the adjutant. "In the left foreleg above the knee. A bullet, no doubt. Congratulations, Count — your baptism of fire!"

Having ridden through smoke past the Sixth Corps, behind the artillery that had been moved forward and was firing — deafening them with its roar — they came to a small wood. There it was cool and quiet, with the smell of autumn. Pierre and the adjutant dismounted and walked up the hill on foot.
"Is the general here?" the adjutant asked on reaching the knoll.
"He was here a minute ago but just went that way," someone told him, pointing to the right.
The adjutant looked at Pierre, as if unsure what to do with him now.
"Don't worry about me," said Pierre. "I'll go up onto the knoll if I may."
"Yes, do. You'll see everything from there and it's less dangerous. I'll come for you."
Pierre went to the battery and the adjutant rode on. They never met again, and only much later did Pierre learn that the adjutant had lost an arm that day.

The knoll Pierre climbed was the famous one later known to the Russians as the Knoll Battery or Raevsky's Redoubt, and to the French as the great redoubt, the fatal redoubt, the redoubt of the center — around which tens of thousands fell, and which the French considered the key to the entire position.
This redoubt consisted of a knoll with trenches dug on three sides. Within the earthworks stood ten guns being fired through openings in the walls.

On both sides of the knoll stood other guns, also firing without pause. A little behind the guns stood infantry. Climbing the knoll, Pierre had no idea that this spot — with its small trenches and handful of guns firing away — was the most critical point of the entire battle.
On the contrary, just because he happened to be there, he thought it one of the least significant parts of the field.

Having reached the knoll, Pierre sat down at one end of the trench surrounding the battery and watched what was happening around him with an unconsciously happy smile. Now and then he stood up and walked about the battery, still smiling, trying not to get in the way of the soldiers who were loading, hauling guns, and constantly running past him with bags and charges. The guns were firing continuously, one after another, with a deafening roar that enveloped the entire area in powder smoke.

In contrast to the dread felt by the infantrymen positioned in support behind them, here in the battery — where a small group of men busy at their work were separated from everyone else by a trench — there was a shared, almost family-like feeling of excitement.

Pierre's unmilitary figure in a white hat made an unfavorable impression at first. The soldiers looked at him sideways with surprise and even alarm as they passed. The senior artillery officer, a tall, long-legged, pockmarked man, moved over to Pierre as if to check the aim of the farthest gun, and studied him with curiosity.
A young round-faced officer, practically a boy, clearly fresh out of the Cadet College and zealously commanding the two guns assigned to him, addressed Pierre sternly.
"Sir," he said, "please step aside. You must not be here."

The soldiers shook their heads disapprovingly at Pierre. But when they had satisfied themselves that this man in the white hat was doing no harm — either sitting quietly on the trench slope with a shy smile, or politely stepping aside for the soldiers as he strolled up and down the battery under fire as calmly as if walking on a boulevard — their hostile distrust gradually turned into a warm, teasing affection, like the kind soldiers feel for their dogs, roosters, goats, and other animals that live with the regiment. They quickly adopted Pierre into their family, gave him a nickname — "our gentleman" — and made fond fun of him among themselves.
A shell tore up the earth two paces from Pierre, and he looked around with a smile as he brushed the dirt it had thrown up from his clothes.
"How is it you're not afraid, sir — really?" a red-faced, broad-shouldered soldier asked Pierre with a grin that showed a set of strong white teeth.
"Are you afraid, then?" said Pierre.
"What do you expect?" the soldier answered. "She's got no mercy! When she comes sputtering down — out go your guts. You can't help being scared," he said, laughing.
Several men with bright, friendly faces stopped beside Pierre. They seemed not to have expected him to talk like a normal person, and the discovery that he did delighted them.
"It's our job as soldiers. But for a gentleman — that's something! There's a real gentleman for you!"
"Back to your posts!" the young officer called to the men gathered around Pierre.
The young officer was clearly performing his duties for the first or second time and therefore treated both his superiors and the men with great precision and formality.

The booming cannonade and rattle of musket fire were growing more intense across the whole field, especially to the left where Bagration's fortifications were, but where Pierre stood the smoke made it nearly impossible to see anything. Besides, his entire attention was absorbed in watching the tight-knit family circle — sealed off from everything else — formed by the men in the battery. His first unconscious surge of joyful excitement from the sights and sounds of the battlefield had now been replaced by a different feeling, especially since he'd seen that soldier lying alone in the hayfield. Now, sitting on the trench slope, he studied the faces around him.

By ten o'clock about twenty men had already been carried away from the battery; two guns were smashed, and cannonballs landed more and more frequently, while spent bullets buzzed and whistled around. But the men in the battery seemed not to notice any of this — cheerful voices and jokes could be heard on all sides.
"A live one!" shouted a man as a whistling shell approached.
"Not this way! Go to the infantry!" added another with loud laughter, watching the shell fly past and fall into the supporting ranks.
"Bowing to a friend, are you?" remarked another, teasing a militiaman who ducked low as a cannonball flew over.
Several soldiers gathered by the trench wall, peering out to see what was happening in front.
"They've pulled back the front line — it's retreated," they said, pointing over the earthwork.
"Mind your own business," an old sergeant shouted at them. "If they've fallen back, it's because there's work for them farther behind."
And the sergeant, grabbing one of the men by the shoulders, shoved him with his knee. This was followed by a burst of laughter.
"To the fifth gun — wheel it up!" came shouts from one side.
"All together now, like bargemen!" came the cheerful voices of the men moving the gun.

"She nearly knocked our gentleman's hat off!" cried the red-faced joker, showing his teeth and teasing Pierre. "Clumsy thing!" he added reproachfully to a cannonball that struck a cannon wheel and a man's leg.
"Come on, you foxes!" said another, laughing at some militiamen who, stooping low, entered the battery to carry away the wounded man.
"Don't like this porridge, do you? Scared crows!" they shouted at the militiamen who stood hesitating before the man whose leg had been torn off.
"Come on, lads... oh, oh!" they mimicked the peasants. "They really don't like it!"
Pierre noticed that after every hit on the redoubt, and after every loss, the liveliness only grew.

Like the flames of a hidden fire leaping more and more vividly from an approaching thundercloud, so — as if in defiance of what was happening — the lightning of an inner fire glowed ever more intensely in the faces of these men.

Pierre didn't look out at the battlefield and didn't care what was happening there; he was entirely absorbed in watching this fire that burned ever more brightly, and he felt it flaming up in the same way in his own soul.

At ten o'clock the infantry that had been in the bushes in front of the battery and along the Kamenka stream retreated. From the battery they could be seen running back past it, carrying their wounded on their muskets. A general and his staff came to the battery, spoke to the colonel, gave Pierre an angry look, and then left, ordering the infantry supports behind the battery to lie flat so as to be less exposed to fire. After this, from among the infantry ranks to the right of the battery came the sound of a drum and shouts of command, and from the battery they could see those infantry ranks moving forward.
Pierre looked over the trench wall and was particularly struck by a pale young officer who, his sword hanging down, was walking backward, glancing around anxiously.

The infantry ranks disappeared into the smoke, but their drawn-out shout and rapid musket fire could still be heard. A few minutes later, crowds of wounded men and stretcher-bearers came back from that direction. Shells began to fall even more frequently on the battery. Several men lay about, not yet removed. Around the cannon, the men moved still more briskly. No one paid attention to Pierre anymore. Once or twice he was shouted at for being in the way. The senior officer strode with big, rapid steps from gun to gun, his face set in a deep frown. The young officer, his face even more flushed, commanded his men with ever greater intensity.
