The soldiers passed up charges, turned, loaded, and performed their tasks with strained precision. They moved with little springy steps, as though walking on springs.

The storm had come upon them, and in every face the fire Pierre had watched kindle now blazed brightly. Pierre stood beside the commanding officer. The young officer, his hand to his cap, ran up to his superior.
"I have the honor to report, sir, that only eight rounds are left. Should we continue firing?" he asked.
"Grapeshot!" the senior officer shouted, without answering the question, looking over the trench wall.
Suddenly something happened: the young officer gasped and, folding double, sat down on the ground like a bird shot on the wing. Everything became strange, confused, and hazy in Pierre's eyes.

One cannonball after another whistled by, striking the earthwork, a soldier, or a gun. Pierre, who hadn't noticed these sounds before, now heard nothing else. To the right of the battery, soldiers were running and shouting "Hurrah!" — but backward, it seemed to Pierre.

A cannonball struck the very end of the earthwork where he was standing, crumbling the earth; a black ball flashed before his eyes and at the same instant plunged into something. Some militiamen entering the battery ran back.
"All grapeshot!" the officer shouted.
The sergeant ran up to the officer and informed him in a frightened whisper — like a butler telling his master that they've run out of a requested wine at dinner — that there were no more charges.
"The scoundrels! What are they doing?" the officer shouted, turning toward Pierre.
The officer's face was red and sweating, his eyes glittering under his furrowed brow.
"Run to the reserves and bring up the ammunition boxes!" he yelled, angrily avoiding Pierre with his eyes and speaking to his men.
"I'll go," said Pierre.
The officer, without answering, strode to the opposite side.
"Don't fire! Wait!" he shouted.
The man who had been ordered to go for ammunition stumbled against Pierre.
"This is no place for you, sir," he said, and ran down the slope.
Pierre ran after him, avoiding the spot where the young officer sat.

One cannonball, another, and a third flew over him, falling in front, beside, and behind him. Pierre ran down the slope. "Where am I going?" he suddenly asked himself when he was already near the green ammunition wagons. He halted in confusion, not knowing whether to return or go on. Suddenly a terrible blast threw him backward to the ground. At the same instant he was blinded by a great flash of flame, and immediately a deafening roar, a crackling and whistling made his ears ring.

When he came to his senses he was sitting on the ground, leaning on his hands; the ammunition wagons he'd been approaching no longer existed — only charred green boards and rags littered the scorched grass. A horse, trailing fragments of its shaft, galloped past, while another lay on the ground like Pierre, uttering long, piercing cries.

title: Book Ten (1812) — Chapter 33
paragraphs: The main action of the Battle of Borodino took place within the seven thousand feet between Borodino and Bagration's fortifications. Beyond that space, there was on one side a demonstration by the Russians with Uvarov's cavalry at midday, and on the other, beyond Utitsa, Poniatowski's clash with Tuchkov; but these were isolated and minor actions compared to what happened in the center. On the field between Borodino and the fortifications, beside the wood, the main action of the day took place in an open space visible from both sides, and was fought in the simplest, most straightforward way.
The battle began on both sides with a cannonade from several hundred guns.
Then, when the entire field was covered with smoke, two divisions — Compans's and Dessaix's — advanced from the French right, while Murat's troops advanced on Borodino from their left.

From the Shevardino Redoubt where Napoleon stood, the fortifications were about two-thirds of a mile away, and it was more than a mile as the crow flies to Borodino, so Napoleon couldn't see what was happening — especially since the smoke mixing with mist obscured the whole area. The soldiers of Dessaix's division advancing toward the fortifications could only be seen until they had descended into the hollow between them and the defenses. Once they entered that hollow, the smoke from guns and muskets grew so dense it hid the entire approach. Through the smoke, glimpses could be caught of something black — probably men — and now and then the glint of bayonets. But whether they were moving or standing still, whether French or Russian, was impossible to tell from the Shevardino Redoubt.

The sun had risen brightly and its slanting rays struck directly into Napoleon's face as, shading his eyes with his hand, he peered at the fortifications. The smoke spread before them, and at times it looked as though the smoke was moving, at times as though the troops were. Shouts could sometimes be heard through the firing, but it was impossible to tell what was actually happening there.

Napoleon, standing on the knoll, peered through a field glass, and in its small circle saw smoke and men — sometimes his own, sometimes Russians — but when he looked with the naked eye, he couldn't tell where what he had just seen actually was.
He descended the knoll and began pacing back and forth before it.
He stopped occasionally, listened to the firing, and stared intently at the battlefield.

But it was impossible to make out what was happening — not only from where he stood below, or from the knoll above where some of his generals had positioned themselves, but even from the fortifications themselves — where by now there were alternately or simultaneously Russian and French soldiers, dead, wounded, living, terrified, or maddened. Even there it was impossible to tell what was going on. For several hours, amid incessant cannon and musket fire, now only Russians were seen, now only Frenchmen, now infantry, now cavalry: they appeared, fired, fell, collided without knowing what to do with each other, screamed, and ran back again.

From the battlefield, adjutants Napoleon had sent out and orderlies from his marshals kept galloping up with reports on the action's progress, but all these reports were false — both because it was impossible in the heat of battle to say what was happening at any given moment, and because many adjutants didn't go to the actual fighting but reported what they'd heard from others, and also because by the time an adjutant had ridden the mile or more to Napoleon, circumstances had changed and his news was already outdated. For example, an adjutant galloped up from Murat reporting that Borodino had been taken and the bridge over the Kolocha was in French hands. The adjutant asked whether Napoleon wanted the troops to cross. Napoleon gave orders to form up on the far side and wait. But before that order was given — almost as soon as the adjutant had left Borodino — the bridge had been retaken by the Russians and burned, in the very skirmish Pierre had witnessed at the start of the battle.

Another adjutant galloped up from the fortifications with a pale, frightened face, reporting that the French attack had been repulsed, Compans wounded, and Davout killed. Yet at the very moment the adjutant had been told the French were beaten back, the fortifications had actually been recaptured by other French troops, and Davout was alive with only a minor bruise. Based on these necessarily unreliable reports, Napoleon issued orders that either had already been carried out before he gave them, or could not and were not carried out.

The marshals and generals, who were closer to the fighting but, like Napoleon, did not participate in the actual combat and only occasionally came within musket range, made their own decisions without consulting Napoleon and issued orders about where and how to fire, where cavalry should charge and infantry should run. But even their orders were rarely carried out, and then only partially. For the most part, things happened contrary to their commands. Soldiers ordered to advance ran back when met with grapeshot; soldiers ordered to hold their ground suddenly rushed forward or backward when Russians appeared unexpectedly before them, and cavalry charged without orders in pursuit of fleeing Russians. In this way two cavalry regiments galloped through the Semenovsk hollow, and as soon as they reached the crest turned around and galloped back at full speed. The infantry moved the same way, sometimes running to entirely different places than ordered. All commands about moving guns, sending infantry to fire, or dispatching horsemen to ride down Russian infantry were given by the officers on the spot nearest the units, without consulting Ney, Davout, or Murat, much less Napoleon. They didn't fear punishment for disobeying orders or acting on their own initiative, because in battle what's at stake is the dearest thing of all — one's own life — and sometimes safety seems to lie in running back, sometimes in running forward. These men in the thick of battle acted on the impulse of the moment. In reality, however, all these movements forward and backward accomplished little harm on their own; the actual damage — the maiming and killing — was done by the balls and bullets flying over the fields where these men floundered about. The moment they left the zone of fire, their commanders in the rear re-formed them, restored discipline, and marched them back into the killing zone, where, under the influence of mortal fear, they broke discipline again and rushed about at random.

title: Book Ten (1812) — Chapter 34
paragraphs: Napoleon's generals — Davout, Ney, and Murat — who were near the zone of fire and sometimes even entered it, repeatedly led huge masses of well-organized troops into the fight. But contrary to what had always happened in their previous battles, instead of news of the enemy's retreat, these orderly formations came back as disorganized, terrified mobs. The generals re-formed them, but their numbers kept shrinking. In the middle of the day, Murat sent his adjutant to Napoleon demanding reinforcements.
Napoleon was sitting at the foot of the knoll, drinking punch, when Murat's adjutant galloped up assuring him that the Russians would be routed if His Majesty would provide one more division.
"Reinforcements?" said Napoleon in a tone of stern surprise, looking at the adjutant — a handsome young man with long black curls arranged like Murat's own — as though he didn't understand the words.
"Reinforcements!" Napoleon thought to himself. "How can they need reinforcements when they already have half the army directed against a weak, unfortified Russian flank?"
"Tell the King of Naples," he said sternly, "that it is not yet noon and I still don't see my chessboard clearly. Go!"
The handsome young adjutant with the long hair sighed deeply without removing his hand from his hat and galloped back to where men were being slaughtered.
Napoleon rose and, summoning Caulaincourt and Berthier, began talking to them about matters unrelated to the battle.

In the middle of this conversation, which was beginning to interest Napoleon, Berthier's eyes turned toward a general with a retinue galloping up the knoll on a lathered horse. It was Belliard. Dismounting, he strode rapidly up to the Emperor and in a loud voice began forcefully arguing the need for reinforcements. He swore on his honor that the Russians were finished if the Emperor would send one more division.
Napoleon shrugged and continued pacing without replying. Belliard began speaking loudly and urgently to the generals gathered around him.
"You are very excitable, Belliard," said Napoleon when he came up to the general again. "In the heat of battle it's easy to make mistakes. Go and have another look, then come back to me."
Before Belliard was out of sight, a messenger from another part of the battlefield galloped up.
"Well, what do you want?" Napoleon asked in the tone of a man irritated at being constantly interrupted.
"Sire, the prince..." the adjutant began.
"Wants reinforcements?" Napoleon said with an angry gesture.
The adjutant nodded and began to report, but the Emperor turned away, took a couple of steps, stopped, came back, and called Berthier.
"We need to commit the reserves," he said, spreading his arms slightly. "Who do you think should be sent?" he asked Berthier, whom he would later call "that gosling I turned into an eagle."
"Send Claparede's division, sire," replied Berthier, who knew every division, regiment, and battalion by heart.
Napoleon nodded in agreement.
The adjutant galloped off to Claparede's division, and a few minutes later the Young Guard, stationed behind the knoll, moved forward. Napoleon watched them silently.
"No!" he suddenly said to Berthier. "I can't send Claparede. Send Friant's division."

Though there was no advantage in sending Friant's division instead of Claparede's — and even an obvious inconvenience and delay in stopping Claparede and dispatching Friant now — the order was executed precisely. Napoleon didn't notice that with his army he was playing the role of the doctor who interferes with his medicines — a role he had so rightly understood and condemned in theory.

Friant's division vanished into the smoke like all the others. From every direction adjutants kept galloping up, and as if by agreement they all said the same thing: they all demanded reinforcements and reported that the Russians were holding their positions and maintaining a hellish fire under which the French army was melting away.
Napoleon sat on a camp stool, lost in thought.
Monsieur de Beausset, the man so fond of travel, having fasted since morning, approached the Emperor and respectfully ventured to suggest lunch to His Majesty.
"I hope I may now congratulate Your Majesty on a victory?" he said.

Napoleon silently shook his head. Assuming the refusal referred only to the victory and not to lunch, Monsieur de Beausset respectfully and playfully observed that there was no reason to skip a meal just because one couldn't get one.
"Go away!" Napoleon exclaimed suddenly and sourly, turning aside.
A blissful smile of regret, repentance, and rapture spread over Monsieur de Beausset's face, and he glided away to join the other generals.

Napoleon was experiencing a depression like that of a perpetually lucky gambler who, after recklessly throwing money around and always winning, suddenly finds — just when he has calculated all the odds — that the more carefully he plays, the more surely he loses.

His troops were the same, his generals the same, the same preparations had been made, the same formations set, and the same brief, forceful proclamation issued. He himself was still the same — he knew it, and knew he was now even more experienced and skilled than before. Even the enemy was the same as at Austerlitz and Friedland — yet the terrible stroke of his arm had somehow supernaturally become powerless.

All the old methods that had always been crowned with success — concentrating batteries on one point, attacking with reserves to break the enemy line, cavalry charges by his "men of iron" — all had been employed. Yet not only was there no victory, but from every direction came the same news: generals killed and wounded, reinforcements needed, the impossibility of driving back the Russians, and disorganization in his own troops.

In the past, after giving two or three orders and uttering a few phrases, marshals and adjutants would gallop up with congratulations and happy faces, announcing captured trophies, columns of prisoners, bundles of enemy flags and standards, cannons and supplies, while Murat only begged permission to unleash the cavalry to sweep up the baggage trains. So it had been at Lodi, Marengo, Arcola, Jena, Austerlitz, Wagram, and elsewhere. But now something strange was happening to his troops.

Despite reports of capturing the fortifications, Napoleon sensed that this was not the same — not at all the same — as his previous battles. He saw that what he was feeling was felt by all the experienced men around him. All their faces looked dejected, and they avoided each other's eyes — only a de Beausset could fail to grasp the meaning of what was happening.

But Napoleon, with his long experience of war, knew very well what it meant when the attacking side fails to win a battle after eight hours and all its efforts have been spent. He knew this was a lost battle, and that the slightest mishap — with things balanced on such a knife's edge — could destroy him and his army.

When he surveyed this entire strange Russian campaign, in which not a single battle had been won and not a flag, cannon, or army corps captured in two months; when he looked at the barely concealed despair on the faces around him and heard that the Russians were still holding their ground — a terrible feeling like a nightmare seized him, and every possible disaster that could destroy him flooded his mind. The Russians might fall on his left flank, might break through his center; he himself might be killed by a stray cannonball. All this was possible. In his previous battles he had only considered the possibilities of success, but now countless unlucky chances presented themselves, and he expected them all. Yes, it was like a dream where a man imagines a thug is coming to attack him, and he raises his arm to strike a terrible blow that should annihilate the attacker — only to feel his arm go limp and powerless like a rag, and the horror of inescapable destruction seizes him in his helplessness.

The news that the Russians were attacking the left flank of the French army aroused exactly that horror in Napoleon. He sat silently on a camp stool below the knoll, his head bowed, elbows on his knees. Berthier approached and suggested they ride along the line to assess the situation.
"What? What did you say?" Napoleon asked. "Yes, tell them to bring my horse."
He mounted and rode toward Semenovsk.

Through the slowly dispersing powder smoke, Napoleon saw horses and men lying in pools of blood, alone or in heaps. Neither Napoleon nor any of his generals had ever seen such horrors or so many killed in such a small area. The roar of guns, which hadn't stopped for ten hours, exhausted the ear and gave a peculiar significance to the scene, like music accompanying a tableau. Napoleon rode up the rise at Semenovsk, and through the smoke saw ranks of men in unfamiliar-colored uniforms. They were Russians.

The Russians stood in solid ranks behind Semenovsk village and its knoll, their guns booming ceaselessly along their line, sending forth clouds of smoke. It was no longer a battle — it was a continuous slaughter, futile for both French and Russians. Napoleon stopped his horse and again fell into the reverie from which Berthier had roused him. He couldn't stop what was going on before him and around him — events supposedly directed by him and dependent on him — and this venture, for the first time, seemed unnecessary and horrible because of its lack of success.

One of the generals rode up and dared to suggest leading the Old Guard into action. Ney and Berthier, standing near Napoleon, exchanged glances and smiled contemptuously at this general's senseless proposal.
Napoleon bowed his head and remained silent for a long time.
"At eight hundred leagues from France, I will not have my Guard destroyed!" he said, and turning his horse, he rode back to Shevardino.

title: Book Ten (1812) — Chapter 35
paragraphs: On the rug-covered bench where Pierre had seen him that morning, Kutuzov sat with his gray head hanging, his heavy body relaxed. He gave no orders — he merely agreed with or overruled what others suggested.

"Yes, yes, do that," he replied to various proposals. "Yes, yes — go, my dear fellow, and have a look," he would say to one or another around him; or, "No, don't — we'd better wait!" He listened to reports and gave directions when his subordinates required them; but while listening, he seemed less interested in the substance of the words than in the expressions and tones of voice of those reporting. Through long years of military experience, he knew — and with the wisdom of age understood — that no single man can direct hundreds of thousands of others locked in a struggle with death, and that the outcome of a battle is decided not by a commander's orders, nor by troop positions, nor by the number of cannons or dead, but by that intangible force called the spirit of the army. He watched that spirit and guided it as best he could.
Kutuzov's general expression was one of concentrated quiet attention, his face strained, as though the fatigue of his old, feeble body was hard to endure.
At eleven o'clock they brought him news that the fortifications captured by the French had been retaken, but that Prince Bagration was wounded. Kutuzov groaned and shook his head.
"Ride over to Prince Peter Ivanovich and find out exactly what's happened," he said to one of his adjutants, then turned to the Duke of Wurttemberg standing behind him.
"Will Your Highness please take command of the First Army?"
Soon after the Duke's departure — before he could possibly have reached Semenovsk — his adjutant returned and told Kutuzov that the Duke was requesting more troops.

Kutuzov grimaced and sent an order for Dokhturov to take command of the First Army, and a request to the Duke — whom he said he couldn't spare at such a critical moment — to return. When they brought news that Murat had been taken prisoner and the staff officers congratulated him, Kutuzov smiled.
"Wait a moment, gentlemen," he said. "The battle is won, and there's nothing extraordinary about capturing Murat. Still, it's better to hold off on celebrations."
But he sent an adjutant to carry the news through the army.

When Shcherbinin came galloping from the left flank with news that the French had captured the fortifications and the village of Semenovsk, Kutuzov — guessing from the sounds of battle and Shcherbinin's expression that the news was bad — stood up as if to stretch his legs and, taking Shcherbinin's arm, led him aside.
"Go, my dear fellow," he said to Ermolov, "and see if something can't be done."

Kutuzov was at Gorki, near the center of the Russian position. The attack Napoleon had directed against the Russian left flank had been repulsed several times. In the center the French had not advanced beyond Borodino, and on their left flank Uvarov's cavalry had routed the French.

Toward three o'clock the French attacks stopped. On the faces of everyone coming from the battlefield and those around him, Kutuzov noticed an expression of extreme tension. He was satisfied with the day's success — which exceeded his expectations — but the old man's strength was failing. Several times his head drooped as if falling, and he dozed off. Dinner was brought to him.

Adjutant General Wolzogen, the man who had told Prince Andrew in passing that "the war should be extended widely" and whom Bagration had so despised, rode up while Kutuzov was eating. Wolzogen came from Barclay de Tolly to report on affairs on the left flank. The shrewd Barclay, seeing crowds of wounded streaming back and the army's rear in disorder, had weighed all the circumstances, concluded the battle was lost, and sent his favorite officer to the commander in chief with that news.
Kutuzov was chewing a piece of roast chicken with difficulty and glanced at Wolzogen with eyes that brightened under their puckered lids.
Wolzogen, casually stretching out his legs, approached Kutuzov with a half-contemptuous smile, barely touching the peak of his cap.

He treated his Serene Highness with a somewhat affected indifference intended to show that, as a highly trained military man, he left it to the Russians to make an idol of this useless old man, while he himself knew exactly who he was dealing with. "The old gentleman" — as the Germans in their circle called Kutuzov — "is making himself very comfortable," Wolzogen thought, and looking critically at the dishes before Kutuzov, he began reporting the situation on the left flank as Barclay had instructed him and as he himself had observed.
"All our positions are in the enemy's hands and we can't dislodge them because there aren't enough troops. The men are running away and it's impossible to stop them," he reported.
Kutuzov stopped chewing and stared at Wolzogen in astonishment, as if not understanding what was being said. Wolzogen, noticing the old man's agitation, said with a smile:
"I did not consider it right to hide from your Serene Highness what I have seen. The troops are in complete disorder..."
"You have seen? You have seen?" Kutuzov shouted. Scowling and rising quickly, he went up to Wolzogen.

"How... how dare you!" he choked, making a threatening gesture with his trembling arms. "How dare you, sir, say that to me? You know nothing about it. Tell General Barclay from me that his information is incorrect and that the real course of the battle is better known to me, the commander in chief, than to him."
Wolzogen was about to reply, but Kutuzov cut him off.

"The enemy has been repulsed on the left and defeated on the right flank. If you have seen poorly, sir, do not allow yourself to state what you don't know! Be so good as to ride to General Barclay and inform him of my firm intention to attack the enemy tomorrow," Kutuzov said sternly.
Everyone fell silent, and the only sound was the heavy breathing of the panting old general.

"They are repulsed everywhere, for which I thank God and our brave army! The enemy is beaten, and tomorrow we shall drive him from the sacred soil of Russia," said Kutuzov, crossing himself, and he suddenly sobbed as his eyes filled with tears.
Wolzogen shrugged, curled his lips, and stepped silently aside, marveling at "the old gentleman's" conceited stupidity.
"Ah, here he is, my hero!" said Kutuzov to a stocky, handsome, dark-haired general who was just climbing the knoll.
This was Raevsky, who had spent the whole day at the most critical part of the Borodino field.
Raevsky reported that the troops were firmly holding their ground and that the French no longer dared to attack.
After hearing him, Kutuzov said in French:
"Then you don't think, like some others, that we must retreat?"
"On the contrary, your Highness — in indecisive battles it is always the most stubborn side that wins," replied Raevsky, "and in my opinion..."

"Kaisarov!" Kutuzov called to his adjutant. "Sit down and write out the order of the day for tomorrow. And you," he continued, turning to another officer, "ride along the line and announce that tomorrow we attack."
While Kutuzov was talking to Raevsky and dictating the order of the day, Wolzogen returned from Barclay and said that the general wanted written confirmation of the order the field marshal had given.

Kutuzov, without looking at Wolzogen, gave instructions for the order to be written out — an order that the former commander in chief, to avoid personal responsibility, very shrewdly wanted in writing.

And through that mysterious, indefinable bond that maintains the same spirit throughout an army — known as "the spirit of the army" and constituting the sinew of war — Kutuzov's words and his order for battle the next day immediately became known from one end of the army to the other.

It was far from the same words or the same order that reached the farthest links of that chain. The stories passing from mouth to mouth bore little resemblance to what Kutuzov had actually said, but the meaning of his words spread everywhere because what he said was not the product of cunning calculation but of a feeling that lay in the commander in chief's soul — as it lay in the soul of every Russian.
And when the exhausted, wavering men learned they were to attack the enemy tomorrow, and heard from the highest command confirmation of what they wanted to believe, they felt comforted and inspired.

title: Book Ten (1812) — Chapter 36
paragraphs: Prince Andrew's regiment was among the reserves that until after one o'clock were stationed idle behind Semenovsk under heavy artillery fire. Toward two o'clock the regiment, having already lost over two hundred men, was moved forward into a trampled oat field in the gap between Semenovsk and the Knoll Battery — where thousands perished that day — and onto which an intense, concentrated fire from several hundred enemy guns was directed between one and two o'clock.

Without moving from that spot or firing a single shot, the regiment lost another third of its men. From the front, and especially from the right, guns boomed ceaselessly through the ever-present smoke, and from that mysterious shroud of smoke that covered the whole forward space, quick hissing cannonballs and slow whistling shells flew without pause. At times, as if to grant them a reprieve, a quarter of an hour would pass during which all the projectiles sailed overhead, but sometimes several men were torn from the regiment in a single minute, and the dead were constantly dragged away and the wounded carried off.

With each fresh blow, the chances of survival for those still standing grew slimmer. The regiment stood in battalion columns three hundred paces apart, but all the men shared the same mood — taciturn and somber. Talk was rare in the ranks and ceased altogether each time the thud of a successful hit was heard with the cry "Stretchers!" Most of the time, on their officers' orders, the men sat on the ground. One, having removed his cap, carefully adjusted and tightened its lining; another rubbed dry clay between his palms to polish his bayonet; another fingered his belt strap and tugged at its buckle; another smoothed and refolded his leg wrappings and put his boots back on. Some built little houses from clods of plowed earth, or braided baskets from the straw in the field. All seemed entirely absorbed in these tasks. When men were killed or wounded, when rows of stretchers passed, or when great masses of the enemy came into view through the smoke, no one paid any attention. But when their own artillery or cavalry advanced, or their own infantry was seen moving forward, approving shouts were heard on all sides. Yet the liveliest interest was drawn to events completely unrelated to the battle — as if the minds of these morally exhausted men found relief in everyday, ordinary things. An artillery battery was passing in front of the regiment. A horse from an ammunition cart got its leg caught over a trace. "Hey, look at that trace horse! Get her leg out! She'll fall! They can't see it!" — the same cries rang out from every part of the regiment. Another time, a small brown dog of unknown origin trotted purposefully in front of the ranks with its tail stiffly upright, until suddenly a shell landed nearby, and it yelped, tucked its tail between its legs, and bolted sideways. Howls and shrieks of laughter erupted across the whole regiment. But such distractions lasted only a moment, and for eight hours the men had been idle, without food, in constant fear of death, and their pale, gloomy faces grew ever paler and gloomier.

Prince Andrew, as pale and grim as everyone else in the regiment, paced back and forth along the edge of the meadow beside the oat field, head bowed, hands clasped behind his back. There was nothing for him to do and no orders to give. Everything went on by itself. The killed were dragged from the front, the wounded carried away, the ranks closed up. If any soldiers ran to the rear, they returned immediately. At first Prince Andrew, considering it his duty to inspire courage, walked among the ranks, but he soon realized this was unnecessary — there was nothing he could teach them. All the powers of his soul, like every soldier's there, were unconsciously focused on avoiding contemplation of the horror of their situation. He walked along the meadow, dragging his feet through the grass and watching the dust on his boots; now he took long strides trying to step in the mowers' footprints; now he counted his steps, calculating how many trips between one strip and another would make a mile; now he plucked wormwood flowers growing along a boundary ditch, crushed them in his palms, and inhaled their sharp, bittersweet scent. Nothing remained of the previous day's thoughts. He thought of nothing. He listened with tired ears to the same recurring sounds, distinguishing the whistle of flying shells from the boom of cannon reports, and glanced at the wearyingly familiar faces of the first battalion's men, and waited. "Here it comes — this one's heading our way again!" he thought, listening to the approaching whistle from the hidden region of smoke. "One, another! Again! It hit..." He stopped and looked at the ranks. "No, it went over. But this one hit!" And again he started trying to reach the boundary strip in sixteen paces. A whizz and a thud! Five paces away, a cannonball tore up the dry earth and disappeared. A chill ran down his back. Again he glanced at the ranks. Probably many had been hit — a large crowd had gathered near the second battalion.
"Adjutant!" he shouted. "Order them not to bunch up."
The adjutant, having carried out the order, approached Prince Andrew. From the other direction, a battalion commander rode up.

"Look out!" came a frightened cry from a soldier, and like a bird whirring in rapid flight and landing on the ground, a shell dropped with little noise within two steps of Prince Andrew and close to the battalion commander's horse. The horse — caring nothing about right or wrong in showing fear — snorted, reared, nearly threw the major, and bolted aside. Its terror infected the men.
"Lie down!" cried the adjutant, throwing himself flat.
Prince Andrew hesitated. The smoking shell spun like a top between him and the prostrate adjutant, near a wormwood plant between the field and the meadow.

"Can this be death?" thought Prince Andrew, gazing with entirely new, envious eyes at the grass, the wormwood, and the thread of smoke curling from the spinning black ball. "I cannot — I do not wish to die. I love life — I love this grass, this earth, this air..." He thought this, and at the same time remembered that people were watching him.
"It's shameful, sir!" he said to the adjutant. "What..."

He didn't finish. Simultaneously came the sound of an explosion, a whistle of splinters like a window frame shattering, a suffocating smell of powder, and Prince Andrew lurched to one side, flung up his arm, and fell on his chest. Several officers ran to him. From the right side of his abdomen, blood was pouring out, forming a large stain on the grass.
The militiamen with stretchers who were called up stood behind the officers. Prince Andrew lay on his chest with his face in the grass, breathing heavily and noisily.
"What are you waiting for? Come on!"
The peasants went up and took him by the shoulders and legs, but he moaned so pitifully that, exchanging glances, they set him down again.
"Pick him up — lift him — it's all the same!" someone cried.
They took him by the shoulders again and laid him on the stretcher.
"Oh God! My God! What is it? The stomach? That means death! My God!" — voices among the officers could be heard saying.
"It flew a hair's breadth past my ear," said the adjutant.
The peasants, adjusting the stretcher to their shoulders, started hurriedly along the path they had worn to the dressing station.
"Keep in step! Those peasants!" shouted an officer, grabbing the peasants by their shoulders to steady them as they walked unevenly, jolting the stretcher.
"Get in step, Fyodor — I mean it, Fyodor!" said the lead peasant.
"That's right!" said the one behind joyfully when he'd matched the step.
"Your excellency! Prince!" said the trembling voice of Timokhin, who had run up and was looking down at the stretcher.
Prince Andrew opened his eyes and looked up from the stretcher, into which his head had sunk deep, then closed them again.

The militiamen carried Prince Andrew to the dressing station at the edge of the wood, where wagons were parked. The station consisted of three tents with their flaps turned back, pitched beside a birch wood. In the wood, wagons and horses stood; the horses were eating oats from their portable troughs, and sparrows flew down to peck at fallen grains. Crows, drawn by the scent of blood, flew among the birch trees, cawing impatiently. Around the tents, over an area of more than five acres, bloodstained men in various uniforms stood, sat, or lay. Crowds of soldier stretcher-bearers with grim, attentive faces stood around the wounded, and the officers trying to keep order couldn't drive them away. Ignoring the officers' commands, the soldiers leaned on their stretchers and stared intently, as if trying to comprehend the difficult problem of what was happening before them. From the tents came now loud, angry cries, now pitiful groans. Occasionally attendants ran out to fetch water or to point out who should be brought in next. The wounded waiting their turn outside the tents groaned, sighed, wept, screamed, cursed, or begged for vodka. Some were delirious. Prince Andrew's bearers, stepping over the unbandaged wounded, carried him — as a regimental commander — close to one of the tents and stopped there, awaiting instructions. Prince Andrew opened his eyes and for a long time couldn't make out what was going on around him. He remembered the meadow, the wormwood, the field, the spinning black ball, and his sudden, passionate rush of love for life. Two steps away, leaning against a branch and talking loudly — drawing everyone's attention — stood a tall, handsome, dark-haired noncommissioned officer with a bandaged head. He'd been wounded in the head and leg by bullets. Around him, listening eagerly, a crowd of wounded men and stretcher-bearers had gathered.

"We kicked him out of there so hard he dropped everything — we grabbed the King himself!" the man cried, his feverish eyes glittering. "If only reserves had come up just then, boys — there wouldn't have been anything left of him! I'm telling you for sure..."

Like all the others near the speaker, Prince Andrew looked at him with shining eyes and felt a sense of comfort. "But isn't it all the same now?" he thought. "And what will be there, and what has there been here? Why was I so reluctant to let go of life? There was something in this life I did not, and do not, understand."

title: Book Ten (1812) — Chapter 37
paragraphs: One of the doctors came out of the tent in a bloodstained apron, holding a cigar between the thumb and little finger of one of his small bloodstained hands so as not to smear it. He raised his head and looked around, above the level of the wounded men. He clearly wanted a brief break. After turning his head from right to left for a while, he sighed and looked down.
"All right, right away," he replied to an attendant who pointed Prince Andrew out to him, and he ordered them to carry him into the tent.
Murmurs arose among the wounded who were waiting.
"So even in the next world only the gentry get a chance!" one of them remarked.

Prince Andrew was carried in and laid on a table that had just been cleared and which an attendant was wiping down. He couldn't make out clearly what was in the tent. The pitiful groans from all sides and the excruciating pain in his thigh, stomach, and back distracted him. Everything he saw around him merged into a single impression of naked, bleeding human bodies that seemed to fill the entire low tent — just as, a few weeks before, on that hot August day, such bodies had filled the dirty pond by the Smolensk road. Yes, it was the same flesh, the same cannon fodder, the sight of which had filled him with horror even then, like a premonition.

There were three operating tables in the tent. Two were occupied, and on the third they laid Prince Andrew. For a while he was left alone and involuntarily witnessed what was happening on the other tables. On the nearest sat a Tatar — probably a Cossack, judging by the uniform tossed beside him. Four soldiers held him down while a bespectacled doctor cut into his muscular brown back.

"Ooh, ooh, ooh!" grunted the Tatar, and suddenly lifting his swarthy, snub-nosed face with its high cheekbones and baring his white teeth, he began to writhe and twist his body, uttering piercing, ringing, drawn-out screams. On the other table, surrounded by many people, a tall, heavyset man lay on his back with his head thrown back. His curly hair, its color, and the shape of his head seemed strangely familiar to Prince Andrew. Several attendants pressed on his chest to hold him still. One large, white, plump leg twitched rapidly with a feverish tremor. The man was sobbing and choking convulsively. Two doctors — one pale and trembling — were silently working on the man's other, blood-soaked leg. When the bespectacled doctor finished with the Tatar, whom they covered with an overcoat, he came over to Prince Andrew, wiping his hands.
He glanced at Prince Andrew's face and quickly looked away.
"Undress him! What are you waiting for?" he said sharply to the attendants.

Prince Andrew's earliest childhood memories came flooding back as the attendant, with sleeves rolled up, began quickly unbuttoning his clothes. The doctor bent over the wound, examined it, and sighed deeply. Then he signaled to someone, and the agonizing pain in his abdomen caused Prince Andrew to lose consciousness. When he came to, the splintered fragments of his thighbone had been extracted, the torn flesh cut away, and the wound bandaged. Water was being sprinkled on his face. The moment Prince Andrew opened his eyes, the doctor bent down, kissed him silently on the lips, and hurried away.

After the suffering he had endured, Prince Andrew experienced a blissful feeling he hadn't known for a long time. All the best and happiest moments of his life — especially his earliest childhood, when he used to be undressed and put to bed, when his nurse would lean over him and sing him to sleep, and he, burying his head in the pillow, felt happy in the sheer awareness of being alive — came back to him, not merely as something past but as something present.
The doctors were busy with the wounded man whose head had seemed so familiar. They were lifting him up, trying to calm him.
"Show it to me... Oh, ooh... Oh! Oh, ooh!" his frightened moans could be heard, subdued by pain and broken by sobs.

Hearing those moans, Prince Andrew wanted to weep. Whether because he was dying without glory, or because he was sorry to leave life, or because of those memories of a childhood that could never return, or because he was suffering and others were suffering and that man beside him was moaning so pitifully — he felt like weeping childlike, gentle, almost happy tears.
The wounded man was shown his amputated leg, caked in dried blood with the boot still on.
"Oh! Oh, ooh!" he sobbed, like a woman.
The doctor who had been blocking Prince Andrew's view stepped aside.
"My God! What is this? Why is he here?" Prince Andrew said to himself.

In the wretched, sobbing, weakened man whose leg had just been amputated, he recognized Anatole Kuragin. Men were supporting him in their arms and offering him a glass of water, but his trembling, swollen lips couldn't grasp its rim. Anatole was sobbing painfully. "Yes, it is him! Yes, that man is somehow closely and painfully connected with me," thought Prince Andrew, not yet clearly grasping what he saw. "What is the connection between that man and my childhood and my life?" he asked himself, finding no answer. And suddenly a new, unexpected memory from that realm of pure and loving childhood came to him. He remembered Natasha as he had first seen her at the ball in 1810, with her slender neck and arms and her frightened, happy face ready for joy — and love and tenderness for her, stronger and more vivid than ever, awakened in his soul. He now remembered the connection between himself and this man who was gazing at him dimly through tears filling his swollen eyes. He remembered everything, and an ecstatic pity and love for that man overflowed his happy heart.
Prince Andrew could no longer hold back and wept tender, loving tears for his fellow men, for himself, and for all their mistakes.

"Compassion, love for our brothers, for those who love us and for those who hate us, love of our enemies — yes, that love which God preached on earth and which Princess Mary taught me and I did not understand — that is what made me sorry to leave life, that is what remained for me had I lived. But now it is too late. I know it!"

title: Book Ten (1812) — Chapter 38
paragraphs: The terrible sight of the battlefield covered with dead and wounded, combined with the heaviness in his head and the news that some twenty generals he knew personally had been killed or wounded, and the awareness that his once-mighty arm was now powerless — all of this had an unexpected effect on Napoleon, who usually liked examining the killed and wounded, considering it a test of his mental strength. Today the horrible appearance of the battlefield overcame that strength. He rode hurriedly from the field and returned to the Shevardino knoll, where he sat on his camp stool — his sallow face swollen and heavy, his eyes dim, his nose red, and his voice hoarse — involuntarily listening, with downcast eyes, to the sounds of firing. With painful dejection he awaited the end of this action in which he considered himself a participant but which he was powerless to stop. A personal, human feeling briefly got the better of the artificial illusion of life he had served for so long. He felt in his own body the suffering and death he had witnessed on the battlefield. The heaviness in his head and chest reminded him that suffering and death were possible for himself too. In that moment he desired neither Moscow, nor victory, nor glory — what need had he for more glory? The one thing he wished for was rest, tranquility, and freedom. But when he had been on the Semenovsk heights, the artillery commander had proposed bringing several batteries up to strengthen the fire on the Russian troops massed before Knyazkovo. Napoleon had agreed and ordered that he be informed of the effect.
An adjutant now came to report that the fire of two hundred guns had been concentrated on the Russians, as ordered, but that they were still holding their ground.
"Our fire is mowing them down in rows, but still they hold on," said the adjutant.
"They want more!" said Napoleon in a hoarse voice.
"Sire?" asked the adjutant, who hadn't heard.
"They want more!" Napoleon croaked, scowling. "Let them have it!"

Even before he gave that order, the thing he didn't want — and for which he gave the order only because he thought it was expected of him — was already being carried out. And he fell back into that artificial world of imagined greatness, and once again — like a horse on a treadmill that thinks it's working for itself — he submissively fulfilled the cruel, grim, inhuman role that fate had assigned him.

And not for that day and hour alone were the mind and conscience darkened of this man, on whom the responsibility for what was happening lay more heavily than on all the others who took part. Never to the end of his life could he grasp goodness, beauty, or truth, or the meaning of his actions — which were too contrary to goodness and truth, too remote from everything human, for him ever to understand. He could not renounce his deeds, praised as they were by half the world, and so he had to renounce truth, goodness, and all humanity.

Not only on that day, as he rode over the battlefield strewn with men killed and maimed — by his will, as he believed — did he count how many Russians there were for each Frenchman and, deceiving himself, find cause for satisfaction in the ratio of five Russians to every Frenchman. Not on that day alone did he write to Paris that "the battlefield was superb" because fifty thousand corpses lay upon it. Even on the island of St. Helena, in peaceful solitude where he said he meant to devote his leisure to recounting his great deeds, he wrote:
The Russian war should have been the most popular war of modern times: it was a war of good sense, for real interests, for the peace and security of all; it was purely pacific and conservative.

It was a war for a great cause — the end of uncertainty and the beginning of security. A new horizon and new work were opening up, full of prosperity for all. The European system was already in place; all that remained was to organize it.

Satisfied on these great points, and with peace everywhere, I too would have had my Congress and my Holy Alliance. Those ideas were stolen from me. In that gathering of great sovereigns we would have discussed our interests like a family and rendered account to the peoples as a clerk does to his master.

In this way Europe would soon have become, in fact, one people, and anyone traveling anywhere would always have found himself in the common fatherland. I would have demanded freedom of navigation on all rivers for everyone, that the seas be common to all, and that the great standing armies be reduced to mere bodyguards for the sovereigns.

Returning to France, to the bosom of this great, strong, magnificent, peaceful, and glorious fatherland, I would have proclaimed its borders unchangeable; all future wars purely defensive, all expansion contrary to the nation's interests. I would have shared the empire with my son; my dictatorship would have ended and his constitutional reign would have begun.
Paris would have been the capital of the world, and the French the envy of the nations!

My leisure and old age would then have been devoted — in the company of the Empress, and during my son's royal apprenticeship — to leisurely visiting every corner of the Empire in our own carriage, like a true country couple, receiving complaints, righting wrongs, and scattering public buildings and benefactions everywhere.

Napoleon, predestined by Providence for the grim role of executioner of nations, convinced himself that the purpose of his actions had been the welfare of peoples and that he could control the fate of millions and bestow blessings through the exercise of power.

"Of the four hundred thousand who crossed the Vistula," he wrote further about the Russian war, "half were Austrians, Prussians, Saxons, Poles, Bavarians, Wurttembergers, Mecklenburgers, Spaniards, Italians, and Neapolitans. The Imperial army, strictly speaking, was one-third composed of Dutch, Belgians, Rhinelanders, Piedmontese, Swiss, Genevans, Tuscans, Romans, inhabitants of the Thirty-second Military Division, of Bremen, of Hamburg, and so on: it included barely a hundred and forty thousand who spoke French. The Russian expedition actually cost France fewer than fifty thousand men; the Russian army in its retreat from Vilna to Moscow lost four times more men in battle than the French; the burning of Moscow cost the lives of a hundred thousand Russians who died of cold and hunger in the forests; finally, on its march from Moscow to the Oder the Russian army also suffered from the brutal weather, so that by the time it reached Vilna it numbered only fifty thousand, and at Kalisch fewer than eighteen thousand."

He imagined that the war with Russia came about by his will, and the horrors that occurred did not shake his soul. He boldly took full responsibility for everything, and his darkened mind found justification in the belief that among the hundreds of thousands who perished, there were fewer Frenchmen than Hessians and Bavarians.

title: Book Eleven (1812) — Chapter 39
paragraphs: Tens of thousands of the slain lay in various positions and uniforms on the fields and meadows belonging to the Davydov family and to the crown serfs — those same fields and meadows where for hundreds of years the peasants of Borodino, Gorki, Shevardino, and Semenovsk had harvested their crops and grazed their cattle. At the dressing stations, the grass and earth were soaked with blood across a space of some three acres. Crowds of men from various units, wounded and unwounded, with frightened faces, dragged themselves back toward Mozhaysk from one army and back to Valuevo from the other. Other groups, exhausted and hungry, pushed forward led by their officers. Still others held their ground and continued to fire.

Over the whole field — previously so gaily beautiful with its glitter of bayonets and cloudlets of smoke in the morning sun — there now spread a mist of dampness and smoke and a strange acid smell of saltpeter and blood. Clouds gathered, and drops of rain began to fall on the dead and wounded, on the frightened, exhausted, and hesitating men, as if to say: "Enough, men! Enough! Stop — think about what you are doing!"

To the men on both sides alike, worn out by hunger and fatigue, it equally began to seem doubtful whether they should keep slaughtering each other; on all faces there was hesitation, and the same question arose in every soul: "For what, for whom, must I kill and be killed? You may go and kill whoever you want, but I don't want to do it anymore!" By evening this thought had ripened in every mind. At any moment these men might have been seized with horror at what they were doing and might have thrown everything aside and run anywhere.

But though toward the end of the battle they all felt the full horror of their actions — though they would have been glad to stop — some incomprehensible, mysterious force continued to control them. They still brought up charges, loaded, aimed, and fired, even though only one artilleryman survived out of every three, and though they stumbled and gasped with fatigue, drenched in sweat, caked in blood and powder. The cannonballs flew just as swiftly and cruelly from both sides, crushing human bodies, and that terrible work continued — not by the will of men but at the will of Him who governs men and worlds.

Anyone looking at the disorganized rear of the Russian army would have said that if the French made just one more small effort, it would collapse completely; and anyone looking at the French rear would have said the Russians needed only one more push to destroy them. But neither the French nor the Russians made that effort, and the flame of battle slowly burned out.

The Russians didn't make that effort because they were not the attackers. At the start of the battle they had stood blocking the road to Moscow, and they were still doing so at the end. But even if the Russians had wanted to drive the French from their positions, they couldn't have made this final push — every part of the Russian army had suffered in the battle. Though still holding their ground, they had lost ONE HALF of their men.

The French, with the memory of fifteen years of victories, with confidence in Napoleon's invincibility, with the knowledge that they had captured part of the battlefield and lost only a quarter of their men, and with their Guards still intact — twenty thousand strong — might easily have made that effort. The French, who had attacked the Russian army to drive it from its position, should have made it, because as long as the Russians continued blocking the road to Moscow, the French objective had not been achieved and all their efforts and losses were wasted. But they did not. Some historians say Napoleon only needed to commit his Old Guard and the battle would have been won. Talking about what would have happened if Napoleon had sent his Guards is like discussing what would happen if autumn turned into spring. It couldn't be. Napoleon didn't hold back his Guards because he didn't want to use them — he held back because it couldn't be done. All the generals, officers, and soldiers in the French army knew it couldn't be done, because the army's flagging spirit would not allow it.

It was not Napoleon alone who had experienced that nightmare feeling of a mighty arm struck powerless; all the generals and soldiers felt the same, whether they had fought in the battle or not. After all their experience of previous battles — when after one-tenth of such effort the enemy had fled — they were seized by a similar terror before an enemy who, after losing HALF his men, stood as threateningly at the end as at the beginning. The moral force of the attacking French army was exhausted. Not the kind of victory measured by captured flags on sticks or possession of ground, but a moral victory — one that convinces the enemy of his opponent's spiritual superiority and of his own impotence — was won by the Russians at Borodino. The French invaders, like an infuriated animal that has received a mortal wound in its charge, felt they were dying but could not stop, just as the Russian army, weakened by half, could not help giving way. By momentum alone the French army could still roll forward to Moscow, but there, without any further effort by the Russians, it would have to perish, bleeding from the mortal wound received at Borodino. The direct consequence of the Battle of Borodino was Napoleon's senseless flight from Moscow, his retreat along the old Smolensk road, the destruction of the invading army of five hundred thousand, and the downfall of Napoleonic France — upon which at Borodino, for the first time, the hand of a spiritually stronger opponent had been laid.

title: Book Eleven (1812) — Chapter 1
paragraphs: Absolute continuity of motion is incomprehensible to the human mind. The laws of any kind of motion become understandable only when we examine arbitrarily selected segments of that motion; but at the same time, a large share of human error comes from this arbitrary division of continuous motion into separate elements. There is a well-known ancient paradox in which Achilles can never overtake a tortoise he is chasing, despite traveling ten times faster. By the time Achilles covers the distance that separated him from the tortoise, the tortoise has moved ahead one-tenth of that distance; when Achilles covers that tenth, the tortoise has moved another hundredth, and so on forever. This problem seemed insoluble to the ancients. The absurd conclusion — that Achilles could never catch the tortoise — resulted from dividing motion into separate segments, when in fact both Achilles' and the tortoise's motion was continuous.

By making the segments smaller and smaller we only approach a solution but never reach it. Only when we accept the concept of the infinitely small, and the resulting geometric series with a ratio of one-tenth, and find its sum to infinity, do we solve the problem.
A modern branch of mathematics, having mastered the art of dealing with the infinitely small, can now solve other, more complex problems of motion that once seemed impossible.

This modern branch of mathematics — unknown to the ancients — admits the concept of the infinitely small when dealing with problems of motion, and thereby conforms to the fundamental condition of all motion (absolute continuity), correcting the inevitable error the human mind makes when it examines separate segments of motion instead of continuous movement.
In seeking the laws of historical movement, exactly the same thing happens. The movement of humanity, arising from countless individual human wills, is continuous.

To understand the laws of this continuous movement is the goal of history. But to arrive at these laws — which result from the sum of all those human wills — the human mind invents arbitrary, disconnected units. The first method of history is to select an arbitrary series of continuous events and examine it in isolation, though there can be no beginning to any event, since one event always flows seamlessly from another.

The second method is to treat the actions of a single person — a king or commander — as equivalent to the sum of many individual wills, when in fact the sum of individual wills is never expressed by the actions of any single historical figure.

Historical science, in its effort to draw closer to truth, takes smaller and smaller units for examination. But however small the units, we sense that treating any unit as disconnected from others, or assuming a beginning for any event, or claiming that one person's actions represent the will of many, is inherently false.

It takes no great critical effort to completely demolish any conclusions drawn from history. One need only select a larger or smaller unit for study — as any critic has every right to do, since whatever unit history examines must always be arbitrarily chosen.

Only by taking infinitely small units for observation — the differential of history, meaning the individual tendencies of men — and mastering the art of integrating them (finding the sum of these infinitesimals) can we hope to discover the laws of history.

The first fifteen years of the nineteenth century in Europe present an extraordinary movement of millions of people. They leave their ordinary lives, rush from one side of Europe to the other, plunder and slaughter one another, triumph and despair, and for several years the entire course of life is disrupted by an intensive movement that first surges and then subsides. What caused this movement? By what laws was it governed? asks the human mind.

The historians, answering this question, present the words and deeds of a few dozen men in a building in Paris, calling these words and deeds "the Revolution"; then they give us a detailed biography of Napoleon and of various people favorable or hostile to him; describe the influence some of these people had on others, and say: that is why this movement occurred, and those are its laws.

But the human mind refuses to accept this explanation and plainly declares that this method is flawed, because a weaker phenomenon is being treated as the cause of a stronger one. The sum of human wills produced the Revolution and Napoleon, and only the sum of those wills first tolerated and then destroyed them.

"But every time there have been conquests there have been conquerors; every time there has been a revolution there have been great men," says history. And indeed, human reason replies: every time conquerors appear there have been wars — but this doesn't prove that conquerors caused the wars, or that the laws of war can be found in the personal activity of a single man. Whenever I look at my watch and its hands point to ten, I hear the church bells next door ring; but because the bells ring when the hands reach ten, I have no right to claim that the movement of the hands causes the bells to ring.
Whenever I see a locomotive move, I hear a whistle and see valves opening and wheels turning; but I have no right to conclude that the whistle and turning wheels cause the locomotive to move.

The peasants say cold wind blows in late spring because the oaks are budding, and indeed every spring cold winds do blow when the oaks bud. But though I don't know what actually causes the cold winds when the buds unfold, I cannot agree with the peasants that the oak buds cause the cold wind, because the force of the wind is beyond the influence of the buds. I see only a coincidence of events — as happens with all phenomena of life — and I see that no matter how carefully I observe the watch hands, the valves and wheels, or the oak buds, I will not discover the cause of the bells ringing, the engine moving, or the spring winds. For that, I must completely change my perspective and study the laws of steam, of bells, and of wind. History must do the same. And attempts in this direction have already been made.

To study the laws of history, we must completely change our focus — set aside kings, ministers, and generals, and study the common, infinitely small elements by which the masses are moved. No one can say how far it is possible to advance this way toward understanding the laws of history; but clearly only along this path does the possibility of discovering those laws lie, and as yet not a millionth part of the mental effort has been applied in this direction that historians have devoted to describing the actions of various kings, commanders, and ministers, and offering their own reflections on those actions.

title: Book Eleven (1812) — Chapter 3
paragraphs: When Ermolov, sent by Kutuzov to inspect the position, reported that it was impossible to fight there before Moscow and that they must retreat, Kutuzov looked at him in silence.
"Give me your hand," he said, and turning it over to feel the pulse, added: "You're not well, my dear fellow. Think about what you're saying!"
Kutuzov could not yet bring himself to accept the possibility of retreating beyond Moscow without a battle.

On Poklonny Hill, four miles from the Dorogomilov gate of Moscow, Kutuzov got out of his carriage and sat down on a bench by the roadside. A large group of generals gathered around him, and Count Rostopchin, who had come from Moscow, joined them. This distinguished company split into several groups, all discussing the advantages and disadvantages of the position, the state of the army, the suggested plans, the situation in Moscow, and military matters generally. Though they hadn't been summoned for that purpose and the gathering wasn't officially called one, they all felt this was essentially a council of war. The conversations all dealt with public affairs. If anyone shared or asked for personal news, it was done in a whisper, and they immediately returned to general matters. No jokes, laughter, or even smiles were seen among these men. They all clearly made an effort to rise to the gravity of the situation. And all these groups, while talking among themselves, tried to stay near the commander in chief — whose bench formed the center of the gathering — and to speak loudly enough for him to hear. The commander in chief listened and sometimes asked them to repeat their remarks, but did not join the conversations or express any opinion. After hearing what one group or another had to say, he generally turned away with a look of disappointment, as though they weren't discussing what he wanted to hear. Some debated the chosen position, criticizing not so much the position itself as the competence of those who'd chosen it. Others argued that a mistake had been made earlier — that a battle should have been fought two days ago. Still others talked about the Battle of Salamanca, described by Crosart, a newly arrived Frenchman in a Spanish uniform. (This Frenchman and one of the German princes serving with the Russian army were discussing the siege of Saragossa and whether Moscow could be defended in a similar way.) Count Rostopchin was telling another group that he was prepared to die with the city militia under the capital's walls, but couldn't help regretting having been kept in the dark — had he known sooner, things would have been different. A fifth group, displaying the depth of their strategic thinking, discussed the direction the troops should now take. A sixth group was talking outright nonsense. Kutuzov's expression grew more and more troubled and gloomy. From all this talk he drew only one conclusion: that defending Moscow was physically impossible — in the fullest meaning of those words — so utterly impossible that if some senseless commander were to order a battle, the result would be chaos, not combat. It wouldn't happen because the commanders not only recognized the position as hopeless, but in their conversations were discussing only what would follow its inevitable abandonment. How could commanders lead their troops into battle on ground they considered impossible to hold? The lower-ranking officers and even the soldiers, who also think, considered the position hopeless as well, and therefore could not fight, fully convinced they would be defeated. If Bennigsen insisted on defending the position and others still debated it, the question was no longer important in itself — it merely served as a pretext for argument and intrigue. This Kutuzov understood perfectly.

Bennigsen, who had chosen the position, warmly displayed his Russian patriotism (Kutuzov could not listen to this without wincing) by insisting that Moscow must be defended. His motive was clear as day to Kutuzov: if the defense failed, blame Kutuzov for bringing the army to the Sparrow Hills without fighting; if it succeeded, claim the credit; if no battle were fought, clear himself of blame for abandoning Moscow. But this intrigue no longer occupied the old man. One terrible question consumed him, and he heard no answer from anyone. The question was: "Have I really allowed Napoleon to reach Moscow, and when did I do so? When was it decided? Was it yesterday when I ordered Platov to retreat? Was it the evening before, when I dozed off and told Bennigsen to issue orders? Or was it earlier still? When, when was this terrible thing decided? Moscow must be abandoned. The army must retreat and the order must be given." To give that terrible order felt to him like resigning command of the army. And not only did he love the power he was used to — the honors given to Prince Prozorovsky, under whom he'd served in Turkey, still stung him — but he was convinced he was destined to save Russia, and that was why, against the Emperor's wishes and by the will of the people, he had been chosen commander in chief. He was convinced he alone could keep command of the army in these difficult circumstances, and that he alone in the whole world could face the invincible Napoleon without fear. He was horrified at the thought of the order he had to give. But something had to be decided, and these conversations around him, growing too free, had to be stopped.
He summoned the most important generals to him.
"My head, good or bad, must decide for itself," he said, rising from the bench, and he rode to Fili where his carriages were waiting.

title: Book Eleven (1812) — Chapter 4
paragraphs: The council of war began at two in the afternoon in the larger, more spacious part of Andrew Savostyanov's hut. The men, women, and children of the large peasant family crowded into the back room across the hallway. Only Malasha — Andrew's six-year-old granddaughter, whom his Serene Highness had petted and given a lump of sugar while drinking his tea — remained perched on top of the brick oven in the main room. Malasha looked down with shy delight at the faces, uniforms, and decorations of the generals, who filed in one by one and sat on the broad benches in the corner beneath the icons. "Grandad" — as Malasha privately called Kutuzov — sat apart in a dark corner behind the oven, sunk deep in a folding armchair, continually clearing his throat and tugging at his collar, which, though unbuttoned, still seemed to pinch his neck. Those entering went up one by one to the field marshal; he shook some hands and nodded to others. His adjutant Kaisarov was about to pull back the window curtain facing Kutuzov, but the old man waved his hand irritably — Kaisarov understood that his Serene Highness did not want his face seen.

Around the peasant's wooden table, on which lay maps, plans, pencils, and papers, so many people gathered that the orderlies brought in another bench and placed it beside the table. Ermolov, Kaisarov, and Toll, who had just arrived, sat on this bench. In the front place, directly under the icons, sat Barclay de Tolly, his high forehead merging into his bald crown. He wore a St. George's Cross around his neck and looked pale and ill — he'd been feverish for two days and was now shivering in pain. Beside him sat Uvarov, rapidly gesturing and sharing information in a low voice, as they all spoke. Plump little Dokhturov listened attentively with raised eyebrows and folded arms. On the other side sat Count Ostermann-Tolstoy, seemingly lost in his own thoughts, his broad head with its bold features and glittering eyes resting on his hand. Raevsky, pushing back the dark hair at his temples as was his habit, glanced alternately at Kutuzov and the door with a look of impatience. Konovnitsyn's firm, handsome, kind face was lit by a tender, mischievous smile. His gaze met Malasha's, and the expression in his eyes made the little girl smile.

They were all waiting for Bennigsen, who was still finishing his excellent dinner under the pretext of inspecting the position. They waited from four until six o'clock and did not begin deliberating all that time, instead talking quietly about other matters.
Only when Bennigsen entered the hut did Kutuzov leave his corner and move toward the table — though not close enough for the candles to light his face.

Bennigsen opened the council with the question: "Are we to abandon Russia's ancient and sacred capital without a fight, or are we to defend it?" A long, general silence followed. Every face was set in a frown, and only Kutuzov's angry grunts and occasional cough broke the quiet. All eyes were on him. Malasha too watched "Grandad." She was closest to him and saw how his face puckered — he seemed about to cry. But this didn't last.

"Russia's ancient and sacred capital!" he suddenly repeated in an angry voice, echoing Bennigsen's words and drawing attention to their false ring. "Allow me to tell you, your excellency, that this question has no meaning for a Russian." He heaved his heavy body forward. "Such a question cannot be asked — it is senseless! The question I have asked these gentlemen to discuss is a military one: Is it better to give up Moscow without a battle, or to accept battle and risk losing the army along with Moscow? That is the question on which I want your opinion." And he sank back in his chair.

The discussion began. Bennigsen did not consider his game lost. Accepting Barclay's view and others' that a defensive battle at Fili was impossible, but imbued with Russian patriotism and love of Moscow, he proposed moving troops from the right to the left flank overnight and attacking the French right the following day. Opinions divided, and arguments were made for and against. Ermolov, Dokhturov, and Raevsky sided with Bennigsen. Whether they felt a sacrifice was necessary before abandoning the capital, or were guided by personal considerations, these generals seemed not to grasp that the council could not change the inevitable course of events, and that Moscow was in effect already abandoned. The other generals understood this, however, and setting aside the question of Moscow, discussed the direction the army should take in retreat. Malasha, keeping her eyes fixed on what was happening, understood the council differently. It seemed to her merely a personal struggle between "Grandad" and "Long-coat," as she called Bennigsen. She saw that they grew angry when they spoke to each other, and in her heart she sided with Grandad. In the middle of the discussion she noticed Grandad give Long-coat a quick, sly glance, and then — to her joy — she saw Grandad say something to Long-coat that shut him up. Bennigsen suddenly reddened and paced angrily up and down. What had stung him so was Kutuzov's calm, quiet remark about the advantage or disadvantage of Bennigsen's plan to move troops by night from the right to the left flank to attack the French right wing.

"Gentlemen," said Kutuzov, "I cannot approve the count's plan. Moving troops in close proximity to the enemy is always dangerous, and military history supports this view. For instance..." Kutuzov seemed to reflect, searching for an example, then with a clear, innocent look at Bennigsen he added: "Oh yes — take the Battle of Friedland, which I believe the count remembers well, and which was... not entirely successful, precisely because our troops were rearranged too close to the enemy..."
A momentary pause followed that seemed very long to everyone.
The discussion resumed, but pauses came frequently and all felt that nothing more remained to be said.
During one of these pauses Kutuzov heaved a deep sigh, as if preparing to speak. Everyone looked at him.

"Well, gentlemen, I see that it is I who will have to pay for the broken crockery," he said, and slowly rising, he moved to the table. "Gentlemen, I have heard your views. Some of you will disagree with me. But I" — he paused — "by the authority entrusted to me by my Sovereign and my country, I order a retreat."
After that the generals began to disperse with the solemn, hushed air of people leaving a funeral.
Some of them, in low voices and in a very different tone from their council speeches, murmured things to their commander in chief.

Malasha, who had long been expected for supper, climbed carefully backward down from the oven — her bare little feet catching on its ledges — and slipping between the generals' legs, she darted out of the room.

After dismissing the generals, Kutuzov sat for a long time with his elbows on the table, thinking always of the same terrible question: "When, when did abandoning Moscow become inevitable? When was it decided? And who is to blame?"
"I did not expect this," he said to his adjutant Schneider when the latter came in late that night. "I did not expect this! I did not think this would happen."
"You should get some rest, your Serene Highness," replied Schneider.
"But no! They shall eat horseflesh yet, like the Turks!" Kutuzov exclaimed without answering, striking the table with his plump fist. "They shall — if only..."
